title: LG Energy Solution launches battery research competition - electrive.com
content:
LG Energy Solution launches the Battery Innovation Contest 2026. Universities and research institutions worldwide can submit proposals for new battery technologies until December 6. The focus includes battery materials, battery management, and AI.
Since 2017, more than 50 research projects have been funded through the competition.
Image: LGES
South Korean battery manufacturer LG Energy Solution is once again seeking research projects with commercial potential as part of its Battery Innovation Contest (BIC). The tenth edition of the competition is open to universities and research institutions worldwide. Applications have been accepted since 29 October via the company’s in-house innovation platform, BRIDGE.
The competition comprises two categories. In the so-called ‘Thematic Call’, LG Energy Solution specifies research topics identified by its own product development departments. According to the company, the number of these topics has been significantly increased for this year’s edition. They range from battery materials and cells to battery management systems (BMS) and applications of artificial intelligence.
In the ‘Open-Topic Call’, researchers can submit their own research approaches from various fields of battery technology. This allows LG Energy Solution to address specific industry challenges while also incorporating new ideas from the research community.
LGES has funded around 50 research projects since 2017
To protect research ideas, LG Energy Solution uses a two-stage application process. Initially, applicants are only required to submit a brief project outline. Full research proposals are requested only after a pre-selection. This approach ensures that applicants not selected in the first round do not have to disclose extensive details of their research prematurely. Submissions and subsequent project management are handled via the BRIDGE platform.
Since the competition’s launch in 2017, LG Energy Solution has supported around 50 research projects, according to the company. Particularly promising approaches can be further developed in the Frontier Research Laboratory (FRL), a collaborative research initiative between the battery manufacturer, universities, and research institutions that provides additional funding and technical support.
As an example of past achievements, LG Energy Solution cites a physics-based model for accelerating calculations in battery management systems, for which a patent application is currently pending. The company also highlights research into a long-life solid-state battery that can operate at room temperature, with results published in the journal
in 2019.
In parallel with funding external research projects, LG Energy Solution is expanding its own battery portfolio. The South Korean manufacturer is reportedly set to supply
novel 46100 cylindrical cells
for future Mercedes-Benz electric vehicles. Production could begin preparations in 2027, with deliveries scheduled to start in 2028. However, these plans have not yet been officially confirmed.
Through this competition, LG Energy Solution aims to strengthen collaboration between industry and academia and accelerate the practical application of new technologies. Research proposals can be submitted until 6 December 2026 via

title: Fraunhofer develops tool for battery recycling - electrive.com
content:
Fraunhofer FFB and RWTH Aachen University have developed an evaluation model for the recycling of lithium-ion batteries. It allows different processes to be compared in terms of their costs and CO₂ emissions.
The model also takes into account regional electricity mixes and the utilization of recycling plants.
Image: Fraunhofer FFB
The calculation model is designed to help recycling companies, technology providers and battery manufacturers evaluate different recycling processes on a uniform basis – both economically and ecologically.
A recent
study by the EU research project Safeloop
highlighted the significant economic challenges in battery recycling. According to the findings, recycling lithium-ion batteries in Europe under the examined conditions currently results in an average loss of around €1.90 per kilogram of battery pack. The researchers identified hazardous goods transport, disassembly and uncertainties in material recovery as key cost drivers.
The new Fraunhofer model focuses on evaluating individual recycling processes. Available methods differ not only in terms of energy consumption and recovery rates but also in how early-stage decisions impact the quality of recovered materials and the effort required in subsequent stages. To capture these relationships, the tool divides the entire recycling chain into individual areas, process steps and technologies using a modular principle. For example, different shredding processes can be compared, and their effects on the further recycling process can be analysed.
Fraunhofer model considers location & utilisation
The tool is based on a database containing information about individual process steps. Users can specify parameters such as material throughput and the composition of the batteries to be recycled, then compile customised process chains.
The model tracks material flows throughout the entire recycling chain and links them to economic and ecological key performance indicators. Factors such as energy consumption, CO₂ emissions, operating and investment costs, and revenue from recovered raw materials are taken into account. Disposal costs, the regional electricity mix, labour costs and plant utilisation can also be incorporated into the calculations.
If individual parameters such as throughput, separation efficiency or recovery rate change, the tool displays the impact on downstream process steps, costs and emissions. This enables the identification of particularly cost- or emission-intensive areas and the examination of various scenarios for scaling up battery recycling industrially.
“With this tool, we aim to make different recycling concepts comparable on a common basis and thereby create a robust foundation for technological and strategic decisions,” explains Benedikt Gruber, a research associate at Fraunhofer FFB. The model can be used both to optimise existing recycling processes and to evaluate new technologies.
The Modular Lifecycle Tool was developed as part of a consortium study involving partners from the recycling industry, plant engineering and consulting. In the future, the evaluation framework is set to be expanded to include additional battery chemistries, regionally differentiated datasets and regulatory scenarios.

title: New Saft tech takes BESS into energy trading, financing – Batteries International
content: French battery maker Saft has launched EnerShift — an integrated system designed to help energy-intensive industries finance, deploy, and optimise the use of battery energy storage. The TotalEnergies-owned company said on November 4 an industrial-scale EnerShift system in use at its Bordeaux site has already demonstrated a reduction in annual electricity costs by around 15%. EnerShift combines BESS tech, energy management expertise, financing options and energy market optimisation into a single integrated solution, Saft said. Depending on customer requirements, Saft said it can support projects from initial feasibility studies and business case assessment through financing solutions, system deployment and long-term operational optimisation. A key differentiator of the service is its ability to unlock additional value from battery assets through participation in electricity markets. By intelligently charging and discharging batteries according to market conditions, industrial sites can optimise energy purchasing, capitalise on price fluctuations and capture the value of energy flexibility without adding operational complexity for site teams. The Bordeaux installation combines a 9MWh BESS with advanced energy management and energy trading capabilities. Combined with additional value created through electricity market participation, the project is expected to pay for itself in around five years. Saft’s ESS sales director Vincent Le Quintrec said: “Many industrial companies understand the operational benefits of energy storage, but financing and profitability often remain barriers to investment. “Our objective is to help customers deploy battery systems but also maximise their economic return throughout the asset’s lifetime.” Batteries International reported in October that Saft had launched new production lines in Bordeaux for solid-state batteries — which the company said made it the first French manufacturer to have the capacity to develop and produce solid-state batteries that use both sulfide and polymer electrolytes at room temperature. title: Australia has ‘building blocks to become battery powerhouse’   – Batteries International
content:
Lithium, News, Other Chemistries
Read Later
Australia's aluminium industry 'could spur production of prismatic cell cans'
Australia has all the ingredients to become a battery manufacturing powerhouse by expanding and investing in the skills, materials and expertise the country has to make key components, according to new analysis.
A study released on November 4 by the country’s national science agency — the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) — looks beyond Australia’s critical-minerals strengths to consider what it would take to turn more local resources into the parts that make up every battery cell.
The study focuses on expertise in advanced manufacturing, battery materials and industrial process assessment, alongside expertise on how battery components and looking at what Australian industry can already do.
Rather than attempting to build every part of a battery industry at once, the study points to two promising first steps — making prismatic battery cell cans from Australian aluminium using an impact extrusion process, and producing copper current collector foil using electrolytic deposition.
According to CSIRO, a practical first step for Australia could be producing prismatic battery cans from aluminium. The country has a strong aluminium industry and experience in manufacturing similar products, including aerosol cans.
The study recommends investing in facilities and production equipment tailored to making battery cans locally.
Meanwhile, electrolytically deposited copper foil can be a viable first priority for establishing a local lithium ion battery manufacturing sector. This would build on Australia’s copper production and refining capability and can be scaled by adding production cells over time, which is less capital-intensive than rolling routes, the study said.
Rebuilding lost or reduced downstream capability will require careful technical, commercial and market analysis, particularly where facilities need high utilisation to be viable, the study said.
However, CSIRO said its analysis shows that Australia is not starting from scratch. The country has the minerals, parts of the industrial base and growing national interest in clean energy manufacturing. With targeted investment, it could turn more local resources into battery components made in Australia, supporting jobs, supply-chain resilience and long-term energy security.
CSIRO researcher Geoff de Looze said: “Australia has many of the building blocks needed for a battery manufacturing sector. The question is where we can take the most practical next steps.
“This work identifies areas where Australian materials, existing industrial capability and targeted investment could come together to create a stronger domestic supply chain.”
Batteries International

earlier this year that Australia’s battery materials recovery sector had the potential to be worth around A$7 billion ($5 billion) to the national economy by 2050.

title: Energy Vault teams with PowerX for multinational BESS projects – Batteries International
content:
Energy Storage, News
Read Later
Rob Piconi (left), chairman, co-founder and CEO of Energy Vault with Masahiro Ito, president and CEO of PowerX
Energy Vault has signed an agreement with Japan-based grid-scale BESS firm PowerX to consider energy storage and datacentre projects in the US, Japan and Australia.
Under the partnership, announced on November 5, the companies will explore the supply of up to 1.5GWh of PowerX’s Mega Power series products for deployment in the US in 2027.
The series comprises three product lines: Mega Power, a containerised BESS; Grid Connector, an all-in-one grid connection package integrating a power conversion system, transformer and switchgear; and Mega Power DC, a scalable modular data centre with built-in large-scale BESS.
PowerX said all systems would be manufactured at its factory in Japan and were designed to meet foreign entity of concern requirements under US law that apply to energy storage projects seeking federal clean energy tax credits.
Demand for energy storage in the US continues to grow, driven by the expansion of datacentres and the integration of renewable energy.
Beyond the US supply, both companies intend to collaborate on the development, financing, construction and operation of BESS and datacentre projects in international markets.
Energy Vault’s portfolio includes proprietary battery, gravity and green hydrogen energy storage technologies. B-Vault is marketed as a suite of fully-integrated lithium ion-based BESS systems designed for reliability, flexibility, and availability.
Earlier this year, Energy Vault agreed a deal to supply battery storage, grid-forming power conversion systems and AI infrastructure control software for a 1.25GW hyperscale datacentre project in Texas.
The company said it would work with an undisclosed partner to jointly develop the integrated, off-grid power systems in a deal worth around $500 million-$600 million.

title: E3 Lithium joins Canada-made lithium-manganese batteries project – Batteries International
content: E3 Lithium has joined a Canadian-Korean consortium to develop a made-in-Canada lithium-manganese rich (LMR) cathode for next-generation EV batteries. The Alberta-based lithium brine developer said on November 3 it had signed up to a research agreement with partners including the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) and Posco America — a subsidiary of South Korean battery manufacturer Posco — under which E3 will be the exclusive lithium carbonate provider. E3, which is receiving C$98,798 ($70,000) in funding from the NRC’s critical battery materials initiative for the project, will produce chemical precursors with Canadian mining firm Manganese X Energy and processing tech company NiVolt Technologies. NRC will carry out downstream synthesis into cathode material and testing in coin cells, while Posco will provide industrial validation of CAM material. E3 said last month it was nearing completion of a facility in Alberta aimed at proving the commercial viability of direct lithium extraction technology. The facility converts oilfield brine into battery-grade lithium carbonate at demonstration scale before the construction of a commercial facility. Chris Doornbos, president and CEO of E3, said: “LMR batteries offer increased energy density and safety with significant cost savings, with LG, Ford, and GM currently pursuing this cathode as an option. We are excited to be working on the next-gen batteries with the NRC.” Batteries International reported last June that Posco subsidiary Posco Future M had broken ground for an LFP cathode materials plant in South Korea targeting the ESS and EV batteries market. CNP New Material Technology, backed by Posco, secondary batteries firm Pino and battery materials producer CNGR, expect to start production of the facility in 2027. Meanwhile, Ontario launched a C$500 million critical minerals processing fund earlier this year to support investment in projects in the province including EV and battery manufacturing. en-year permit covers the planned 10,000-tonne-per-year Phase 1 in Conneaut, Ohio
First sales of synthetic graphite anode material targeted for Q4 2028
The Export-Import Bank of the United States (“EXIM”) has issued an amended non-binding Letter of Interest (“LoI”) of US$1.4 billion for the G1 AAM facility.
The EXIM AAM LoI is one of two received by G1, bringing total EXIM LoI support to US$2.07 billion
G1 has provided samples to prospective U.S. battery and Energy Storage System customers for testing and qualification purposes
VANCOUVER, BC, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Graphite One Inc. (TSXV: GPH) (OTCQX:
Graphite One
” or the “
“) has received the final air permit from the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency (“
Ohio EPA
“) for Phase 1 of its planned active anode material (“
“) facility in Conneaut, Ohio (the “
Ohio Facility
“), a 10,000 tpy blending and coating plant (the “
Phase 1 Plant
“). The Air Pollution Permit-to-Install and Operate, Permit No. P0140891 (the “
“), was issued to Graphite One (Ohio) Inc.
Anthony Huston,
President and Chief Executive Officer, said :
Receiving the final Ohio Air Permit is an important step toward establishing a domestic synthetic anode material supply chain,
“This approval advances Phase 1 Plant toward first revenue and supports our goal of becoming the first U.S. company commercially producing synthetic graphite anode material.”
The Ohio Air Permit is the key environmental permit required to build and run the Phase 1 Plant, and the one permit the Company has considers the most demanding to receive. AAM is the primary material in the anode of lithium-ion batteries that power electric vehicles and all types of grid energy storage. The Company believes the Phase 1 Plant will be the first of its kind in the U.S.
Key Highlights
Air Permit in hand.
Issued and effective October 27, 2026. Valid to October 27, 2036, renewable.
Full scope, built-in controls.
Covers four emissions units: agglomeration (P001), carbonization (P002), feeding and blending (P901), and finishing and packaging (P902). Thermal oxidizers are designed for 98% control of volatile organic compounds and 99% control with baghouses of particulate matter control.
Ohio EPA review complete.
The Air Permit concludes the technical review announced on July 16, 2026. The Phase 1 Plant now moves toward a final investment decision: 10,000 tonnes per year of planned capacity at an estimated initial capital cost of US$80 million, to be updated after final engineering.
Early Path to Revenue:
First synthetic graphite AAM sales from the Phase 1 Plant are targeted for Q4 2028, subject to a final investment decision, financing, and construction. Graphite Creek mine production is targeted for 2030.
Federal backing.
EXIM has issued an amended, non-binding LoI of US$1.4 billion for the AAM facility to support a phased increase in production capacity, in 25,000 tonne increments to 100,000 tonnes per year of AAM.  The EXIM LoI is one of two received by G1, bringing total EXIM LoI support to US$2.07 billion.
Mike Schaffner,
Chief Operating Officer, said :
Securing the final permit reflects the quality of our engineering and permitting work after a rigorous review by Ohio EPA,
“Our focus now turns to engineering, procurement and financing to bring Conneaut to construction.”
Graphite One has provided samples to prospective U.S. battery and Energy Storage System customers for testing and qualification purposes.
The Market: Commercial and Strategic
U.S. graphite demand is projected to grow more than 600%, to nearly 700,000 tonnes per year by 2034
. China dominates global anode material processing and has imposed export controls on graphite and anode technologies
, making domestic supply strategically important.
Next Steps
Graphite One will now complete final engineering on the Phase 1 Plant. The remaining approvals are standard building, construction, and operating permits from state and local agencies, which follow final engineering and precede construction. The Company intends to pursue these permits on an expedited basis, working closely with those agencies. Under the Air Permit, construction must begin within 18 months of October 27, 2026, with one possible 12-month extension. In parallel, the Company will pursue project financing, including through EXIM, and order long-lead equipment to accelerate the schedule.
Targeted milestones:
The Bigger Picture: Mine to Battery Material
Graphite One is building a vertically integrated U.S. graphite supply chain: from the Graphite Creek deposit near Nome, Alaska, to AAM manufacturing at the Ohio Facility. The U.S. Geological Survey ranks Graphite Creek as the largest graphite deposit in the U.S. and one of the largest in the world
. Mine construction is targeted for 2028 and production for 2030. Under the federal FAST-41 timetable, a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers permit decision on Graphite Creek is targeted by September 30, 2027.

Fire hazard in electric cars: Why manufacturers may be obligated to take them back
EU product safety law could obligate manufacturers of electric cars with dangerous high-voltage batteries to take back the vehicles. In a ruling dated October 16, 2026, and obtained by Dr. Stoll & Sauer, the Offenburg Regional Court, in a case concerning a Cupra Born, expressly considers claims against SEAT to be possible under Article 37 of the EU Product Safety Regulation (Case No. 2 O 356/25). The consumer law firm sees this as an important avenue for those affected whose battery problems persist despite the recall and offers a free initial assessment via its
online e-mobility check
The Offenburg Regional Court cites Article 37 of the EU Product Safety Regulation as a possible basis for a claim against SEAT.
In the case of safety recalls, in addition to repair and replacement, claims for reimbursement may also be considered.
Dr. Stoll & Sauer has already won favorable rulings against Mercedes and Ford.
What the EU regulation stipulates regarding safety recalls
Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2023/988 requires “effective, free and timely remedies” in the case of product safety recalls. The company responsible for the recall must, in principle, offer consumers at least two of these options:
Repair of the recalled product.
Replacement with a safe product of the same type with at least the same value and quality.
Reimbursement of the value, at least equal to the purchase price paid.
Under certain conditions, only one remedy may be offered, for example, if alternatives are impossible or disproportionately expensive. If repair or replacement is not completed within a reasonable time and without significant inconvenience, the regulation provides for a right to reimbursement.
According to Dr. Stoll & Sauer, this could be an additional avenue for affected motorists if a permanent solution is not forthcoming. Whether Article 37 is applicable to a specific vehicle must be examined. This also concerns timing issues for older vehicles: the regulation has been in effect since December 13, 2024.
Offenburg Regional Court sees potential claims against SEAT
The Offenburg case concerns a Cupra Born and the 93S4 battery recall. According to the database extract evaluated by the court, defective battery modules can lead to reduced range and a risk of fire. The court considers both claims under sales law against the seller and claims against SEAT as the manufacturer to be possible.
Regarding the claims against SEAT, the ruling explicitly refers to “Article 37 of Regulation (EC) No 2023/988” in addition to German product safety law. For Dr. Stoll & Sauer, this is an important indication, as the court is thereby considering an additional basis for taking action against the manufacturer.
This does not yet constitute a conviction. The defendants have until November 6, 2026, to respond to the notice.
Battery recalls affect several manufacturers
Problems with high-voltage batteries are already keeping the law firm busy in numerous cases. The recalls and proposed solutions vary depending on the manufacturer and vehicle.
Mercedes EQA and EQB: According to information from the KBA (German Federal Motor Transport Authority) dated August 17, 2026, the timeframe for the battery replacement recall has been extended to March 1, 2028. This does not mean that every affected customer has to wait that long.
Ford Kuga Plug-in Hybrid: Recall 25SC4 concerns potential internal short circuits and fire hazards. The software update may reduce the usable battery capacity.
Cupra Born: In addition to recall 93S4, which is the subject of proceedings before the Offenburg Regional Court, a KBA (Federal Motor Transport Authority) extract dated October 19, 2026, which is available to the law firm, documents campaign 93W4 due to potential overheating during fast charging. Initially, a charging limit of 80 percent is planned; if necessary, battery modules or the entire high-voltage battery will be replaced.
Positive rulings against Mercedes and Ford
Dr. Stoll & Sauer has already won several first-instance rulings in favor of car buyers due to battery problems:
Stuttgart Regional Court, judgments of July 30, 2026, case nos. 53 O 3/26 and 53 O 27/26: Reversal of Mercedes EQA purchases due to the specific fire risk.
Dortmund Regional Court, judgment of September 4, 2026, case no. 3 O 300/25: Reversal of the sale of a Mercedes EQA 250+ against payment of €37,843.35. The judgment is not yet legally binding.
Regional Court Regensburg, default judgment of July 27, 2026, case no. 84 O 872/26: Return of a Ford Kuga and refund of the purchase price less compensation for use. Ford initially failed to file a timely defense and has since filed an objection. The proceedings continue.
These decisions do not constitute a final clarification of the claims under Article 37. However, they show that affected buyers can have their legal options reviewed even during an ongoing recall.
What options affected buyers can have checked
The decisive factors are the specific recall impact, previous workshop measures, and any remaining restrictions. Depending on the case, the following options, in particular, may be considered:
Withdrawal from the purchase agreement and reversal of the transaction with the seller.
Reduction of the purchase price or compensation for damages, if the respective conditions are met.
Additional claims against the person responsible for the safety recall, in particular under Article 37 of the EU Product Safety Regulation.
A recall does not automatically entitle you to return your car. Dr. Stoll & Sauer will assess what claims exist and against whom they are directed. Affected individuals can use the free initial assessment in the
online e-mobility check
Dr. Stoll & Sauer is one of the leading consumer law firms.
Dr. Stoll & Sauer represents consumers in matters including issues with electric vehicles, lease returns, and COVID-19 emergency aid. The firm’s partners co-led the model declaratory action against Volkswagen on behalf of the Federation of German Consumer Organizations (VZBV) and negotiated a settlement of €830 million for approximately 260,000 consumers. Lawyers from the firm also represent plaintiffs in the class action lawsuit concerning the Facebook data breach. The JUVE Handbook 2019/2020 recognized the firm as a market leader for its expertise in managing mass litigation.

Webasto – Battery division up for sale – possible partial IPO in India
Webasto is celebrating its 125th anniversary with high debts. One co-owner draws a bitter conclusion. But two steps could bring the struggling company a lot of money.
Stockdorf. The look back was bitter.
Werner Baier,
supervisory board member and great-grandson of the founder, on Thursday at the 125th anniversary celebration of the struggling automotive supplier, said :
We have lost sight of some Webasto virtues in the last ten years,
The company had expanded too aggressively into new markets and business areas on a debt-driven basis, failing to rely on partnerships as it had in the past and concentrating too much power in its headquarters. The result: Webasto is now “under the control of creditors.”
The anniversary celebration of the sliding and glass roof specialist in Stockdorf near Munich was therefore a low-key affair. However, there is also positive news.
Following the agreement on a refinancing package with banks and car manufacturers
last year and stable business, debt reduction could progress faster than planned thanks to two key steps.
Firstly, the company is on the verge of selling its rapidly growing battery division, which most recently generated €300 million in revenue. CEO Jörg Buchheim stated that they are in close talks with two strategic buyers and that an agreement could be reached before the end of the year.

title: Startup EDENenergy: Used E-Scooter Batteries Become Industrial Energy Storage System - Batteries News
content:
Startup EDENenergy: Used E-Scooter Batteries Become Industrial Energy Storage System
In Germany alone, about one million high-performance batteries from e-bikes and scooters end up in the trash prematurely every year, even though they often still retain a large portion of their capacity. At the same time, stationary energy storage systems are expensive and resource-intensive to manufacture. The Freiburg-based startup EDENenergy solves both prob-lems: It develops modular industrial storage systems from second-life batteries that are high-performance, cost-effective, and sustainable. Former researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE have developed a system featuring interchangeable battery modules and flexible power electronics that efficiently and safely combine heterogeneous batteries into stationary storage systems.
In the field of car batteries, “second-life” concepts have already demonstrated just how valuable used energy storage devices can be. The potential of micromobility—that is, the millions of e-bikes and e-scooters, an increasing number of which are being returned—has not yet been tapped. This is due to the enormous variety of batteries—designs, cell types, energy management systems—which make standardized reuse difficult. This is where the startup EDENenergy comes in with power electronics developed at Fraunhofer ISE:
Florian Bierwirth
, who, like his co-founders Daniel Seeger and Hannes Kurzmann, previously worked in the Power Electronics Department at Fraunhofer ISE, explains :
It allows different storage units to be connected and enables communication with various modules without having to disassemble the batteries,
To enter the market, the startup is focusing on industrial storage systems with a capacity of 70 kilowatt-hours. “In mid-October, we delivered the first storage system to a customer, which was an important milestone for our young company. With this storage size, we initially aim to target medium-sized companies in the region that have a photovoltaic system but do not yet have a storage solution.” The storage systems could also be of interest to municipal utilities, which can use them to optimize self-consumption, smooth out peak loads, or for electricity trading.
For the first industrial storage system, 112 second-life e-scooter batteries—after being thoroughly tested during an initial screening—will be interconnected. Currently, EDENenergy relies on large suppliers (such as e-bike and e-scooter fleet operators), which ensures that enough batteries of the same type are available to start with. In the future, thanks to innovative power electronics, different types of batteries will also be interconnected.
Florian Bierwirth,
outlining the challenge, says :
To do this, the connector interfaces, battery management system, and communication protocols must be adapted for each new battery. There’s a particularly wide range of options when it comes to e-bikes,
In the long term, he notes, standardized communication protocols for battery storage systems and “second-life” legislation governing the use of mobile batteries in stationary applications will be necessary.
The first 350 batteries tested held a pleasant surprise for the three young entrepreneurs: they were in significantly better condition than expected. While EDEN-energy had estimated a remaining capacity (“State of Health”) of 80 percent for second-life batteries, the used batteries actually had an average remaining capacity that, in some cases, was well over 90 percent. In stationary storage systems, where—unlike in their first life—they are exposed to fewer vibrations or temperature fluctuations, these batteries can continue to perform well for several more years. EDEN-energy remotely monitors the battery modules via a monitoring system. When they reach the end of their service life, the battery modules are replaced individually, which can be done even while the battery system is in operation. The batteries that are finally at the end of their useful life are then sent for recycling by partner companies. Compared to standard energy storage systems on the market, this turns an apparent disadvantage into a technical advantage: replacing individual modules makes it possible to maintain the storage system’s capacity at a constant 70 kWh even after 10 years. Due to battery degradation, conventional manufacturers typically guarantee only 80 percent of the original capacity after 10 years.
In the next steps, the young company—which now employs three part-time staff members in addition to its three founders—plans to expand the storage capacity to up to 300 kWh. They are also looking for additional pilot customers among regional businesses that can receive 50 percent funding for the storage system through the state grant program “Mittelstand trifft Start-ups,” which has already been approved. EDENenergy also receives funding from the Center of Excellence for Sustainability and through the state grant program for innovative startups “BW Pre-Seed,” under which JobRad founder Ulrich Prediger is the company’s first investor.

title: Rio Tinto celebrates opening of $1,4 billion lithium projects in Argentina - Batteries News
content:
Rio Tinto celebrates opening of $1,4 billion lithium projects in Argentina
CATAMARCA, Argentina–(BUSINESS WIRE)– President of Argentina Javier Milei and Catamarca Governor Raúl Jalil today joined Rio Tinto Chief Executive Simon Trott to celebrate a major milestone for Argentina’s lithium industry, marking the official opening of Rio Tinto’s Fénix 1B expansion and Sal de Vida operation in Catamarca following a combined investment of around $1.4 billion.
Both projects achieved first production in the second quarter ahead of plan and are now ramping up production. They will add 25,000 tonnes of annual lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) capacity once fully ramped up, strengthening Rio Tinto’s standing and Argentina’s position as a leading supplier of lithium for global markets.
The celebrations included a visit to Fénix by President Milei and Governor Jalil, hosted by Simon Trott, and an inauguration event recognising both projects with national and provincial authorities, employees, suppliers and representatives of local and Indigenous communities.
Javier Milei
, President of Argentina said:
The expansion of the Fénix project is a historic milestone that demonstrates the potential of Argentina’s mining sector.
“This was made possible by the country once again creating incentives for the production of resources that are essential to the modern world.
We are proud that a company of this scale once again sees Argentina as a reliable partner and is investing in our country, validating the decisions we have taken over the past few years.”
Simon Trott,
Rio Tinto Chief Executive said:
Today is a proud moment for Rio Tinto and an important milestone for Argentina’s lithium industry, as we grow our position as a leading global supplier.
“It was a privilege to welcome President Milei, Governor Jalil and national and provincial authorities, and I thank them for joining us to recognise the work behind Fénix 1B and Sal de Vida. These two projects build on nearly three decades of lithium production in Catamarca and the expertise of our Argentine workforce. They demonstrate our industry-leading project delivery capability, as we execute with discipline towards our global target of 200,000 tonnes lithium carbonate equivalent annual production capacity by 2028. The delivery of these projects reflects the dedication of our people, the capabilities of Argentine suppliers and our partnerships with local communities and governments. Our focus now is on safely ramping up production, delivering reliable, high-quality lithium to our customers, and creating lasting value for our shareholders and Argentina.”
Fénix began operations in 1997 as Argentina’s first commercial lithium operation. The Fénix 1B expansion adds 10,000 tonnes of annual LCE capacity to the existing operation, increasing its total target of annual LCE capacity to approximately 40,000 tonnes.
Sal de Vida is a new lithium carbonate operation located approximately 20 kilometres northeast of Fénix, with a target of annual LCE capacity of 15,000 tonnes.
The projects form part of Rio Tinto’s growing lithium business in Argentina, which includes operations and projects across Catamarca, Jujuy and Salta, including the Rincon lithium project.
Rio Tinto’s growth in Argentina is strengthening the country’s supplier network. Around 70% of the approximately $4 billion in growth capital to be invested across our lithium operations in Argentina is expected to be spent with local suppliers.

title: Australia has the ingredients to build a local battery manufacturing sector - Batteries News
content:
Australia has the ingredients to build a local battery manufacturing sector
With electrification of our transport, energy system and industry driving global demand in batteries, new analysis reveals Australia already has the capacity to become a battery manufacturing powerhouse.
The future of Australian battery manufacturing: Cell cans and current collector foils
, by Australia’s national science agency, CSIRO, identifies where local industry has the skills, materials and expertise to make key components for lithium-ion and emerging sodium-ion batteries.
The report looks beyond Australia’s critical-minerals strengths to ask a more practical question: what would it take to turn more of those local resources into the parts that make up every battery cell?
CSIRO Advanced Battery Manufacturing lead, Dr Adam Best, said the work combines expertise in advanced manufacturing, battery materials and industrial process assessment, bringing together knowledge of how battery components are made with a practical understanding of what Australian industry can already do.
“That combination is central to the report’s message that Australia’s battery opportunity is not only about what lies in the ground, but what can be made here from it,” Dr Best said.
McKinsey analysis
projects the global lithium-ion battery value chain could grow to more than US$400 billion by 2030, while the Australian Government’s National Battery Strategy notes that 96 per cent of the total revenue opportunity is expected to occur downstream of mining. Today, much of that value is captured offshore, with the bulk of our critical minerals being exported. CSIRO’s work shows Australia has a pathway to change that story by building sovereign capability in selected parts of the battery supply chain.
Bringing more of the value chain onshore would mean Australia could move beyond exporting raw and refined materials alone, towards creating higher-value products, supporting skilled manufacturing jobs and strengthening supply chains for technologies that will underpin the clean energy transition,
Rather than attempting to build every part of a battery industry at once, the report points to two promising first steps: making prismatic battery cell cans from Australian aluminium using the impact extrusion process, and producing copper current collector foil using electrolytic deposition.
Both opportunities align with Australia’s aluminium and copper resources and its metal-forming, packaging, electrorefining and electrowinning expertise.
CSIRO researcher Geoff de Looze said the study focused on realistic opportunities to move from minerals and materials into higher-value components.
Mr de Looze
Australia has many of the building blocks needed for a battery manufacturing sector,
“The question is where we can take the most practical next steps. This work identifies areas where Australian materials, existing industrial capability and targeted investment could come together to create a stronger domestic supply chain.”
Battery cell cans are the thin metal cases housing a cell’s active parts. Although apparently simple, they must withstand internal pressure changes and crash loads, remain compatible with electrolyte chemicals, minimise weight and leave maximum space for energy storage – all at low cost. Australia could feasibly make any of the cylindrical, prismatic or ‘blade’ cell formats, although some pathways would require major investment in production of nickel-plated steel and aluminium sheet.
A practical first step for Australia could be producing prismatic battery cans from aluminium. Australia already has a strong aluminium industry and experience manufacturing similar products, including aerosol cans. The report recommends investing in facilities and production equipment tailored to making battery cans locally.
A battery’s current collector foils support the cell’s electrochemical core and carry current to its terminals. The copper foil on a lithium-ion battery’s negative electrode is typically just six microns thick – about one-tenth the thickness of a human hair – while the aluminium foil on the other side is about twice as thick. These highly engineered components are critical to battery performance, safety and production.
The report identifies electrolytically deposited copper foil as a viable first priority for establishing a local lithium-ion battery manufacturing sector. It would build on Australia’s copper production and refining capability, can be scaled by adding production cells over time, and is less capital-intensive than rolling routes.
Australia is already a critical minerals powerhouse, but the next opportunity is to capture more value through manufacturing,
“By focusing on practical, technically achievable steps, Australia can build capability, support industry growth and contribute to more resilient battery supply chains both domestically and internationally.”
Rebuilding lost or reduced downstream capability will require careful technical, commercial and market analysis, particularly where facilities need high utilisation to be viable. But CSIRO’s analysis shows that Australia is not starting from scratch. It has the minerals, parts of the industrial base and growing national interest in clean energy manufacturing. With targeted investment, it could turn more local resources into battery components made here, supporting jobs, supply-chain resilience and long-term energy security.
With this in mind, CSIRO has recently established the Australian Battery Safety Facility (ABSF), strengthening Australia’s capability to test and understand battery safety as the country builds its domestic battery industry. The facility will play an important role in supporting a safe and competitive local lithium-ion battery manufacturing sector, helping Australian-made battery technologies meet the performance and safety expectations needed for domestic and international markets.
The future of Australian battery manufacturing: Cell cans and current collector foils report
was funded through the AU-USA Battery R&D Grant, an Australian Government-supported initiative.

content:
Melbourne battery innovation moves towards local manufacturing with ARENA support
A Melbourne-developed battery that can power a home or be taken on the road, is moving towards local
production, with $6.77 million in support from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA).
The $19.35 million project will see Clutch Industries establish and operate a scalable manufacturing line
in Coburg North, Victoria for its PowerNet battery, incorporating semi-automated assembly, testing,
quality assurance and product traceability.
The portable PowerNet is an innovative energy platform centred around a modular 4 kWh battery using
solid-state battery cells. The solid-state battery architecture delivers a safer, lighter and a more compact
energy storage system which fits more energy into a compact battery pack, making them well-suited to
use at home or on the move. The units can be combined to form a household energy storage system or
used individually to power caravans, 4WDs, boats and other off-grid applications.
The project is expected to help move the technology from product development into scalable Australian
manufacturing. Testing will also provide practical evidence about the battery’s real-world performance.
ARENA CEO Darren Miller said the project was an opportunity to turn promising battery technology into
Australian manufacturing capability.
Mr Miller
A battery that can support a household and then be taken on the road shows how flexible and
innovative energy storage technology is becoming,
“ARENA’s support will help Clutch Industries move from product development into scalable local
manufacturing, while testing the PowerNet battery in different real-world settings to get crucial
performance data. Projects like this can build Australian manufacturing skills and give locally developed energy
technologies the opportunity to demonstrate their value at commercial scale.”
Brad Davis,
Clutch Industries CEO, said:
Clutch Industries has a long history of Australian manufacturing, and through our Density battery business, we’re building on that experience to develop next generation energy storage solutions right here in Australia.
ARENA’s support will help us take the next major step in scaling up local battery manufacturing. Our vision for Density goes well beyond a single product. We’re unlocking product innovation, using breakthroughs in battery technology to create solutions that were previously impractical or simply not possible. With Density products already available through major Australian retailers, we’re excited to continue expanding the brand, growing our manufacturing capabilities and bringing Australian-developed battery
technology to more consumers.”
The project is being supported through the Battery Breakthrough Initiative. For more information, visit

title: ISU Specialty Chemical and Ares Materials to Co-Develop Polymer Materials for Solid-State Batteries - Batteries News
content:
ISU Specialty Chemical and Ares Materials to Co-Develop Polymer Materials for Solid-State Batteries
Partnership pairs ISU’s lithium sulfide and specialty-chemical production with Ares’ closed-loop AI framework for application-driven formulation
PLANO, Texas and SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — ISU Specialty Chemical, a lithium sulfide producer and member of Korea’s ISU Group, and Ares Materials, a materials-AI company based in Plano, Texas, and Guadalajara, Mexico, said Wednesday they will jointly develop polymer materials for solid-state batteries, along with the AI tools used to optimize them.
Under the agreement, Ares will develop the polymer formulations and the AI framework used to tune them against cell-level battery test data. ISU will contribute its specialty-chemical and lithium sulfide manufacturing and lead production and commercial supply.
Developing polymers for solid-state cells typically requires building and cycling test cells for each change to a formulation. Battery makers have cited the length of that cycle, and the difficulty of attributing a result to a specific ingredient or process step, as a constraint on commercialization timelines. Cell specifications also continue to change as the technology matures, so a formulation qualified against one target is often re-opened when the target moves.
AI tools for materials fall broadly into two categories: discovery, which screens candidate molecules to identify new materials, and formulation optimization, which adjusts the composition and processing of a chosen chemistry until it meets targets in a working device. The partnership covers the second. According to Ares, its framework is trained on measured device-level performance and decomposes each test result into the contribution of individual formulation and process variables, then uses that model to select the next set of experiments. The companies said the performance data and models generated in developing the first material will carry forward into the next generations of the product, so that each one starts from an existing performance model rather than from scratch.
Liz Lee,
Associate Director at Counterpoint Research, said :
The combination of AI-based materials intelligence and established specialty-chemical manufacturing can help address a key industry challenge: developing and commercializing better materials with fewer iterations and less time,
“As battery and electronics manufacturers seek improved performance, partnerships connecting predictive materials design with industrial-scale expertise could become an important source of competitive advantage, particularly for next-generation battery materials where quality, cost and scalability are critical.”
ISU Specialty Chemical, a member of Korea’s ISU Group, reported 2025 revenue of approximately ₩411.5 billion (about US$290 million). It produces molecular-weight regulators, including TDM, NOM and NDM, and completed a commercial lithium sulfide plant this year. ISU Group, headquartered in Seoul, dates to the founding of ISU Chemical in 1969; its three listed affiliates reported combined 2025 revenue of more than ₩3 trillion (about US$2.2 billion).
Lyu Seung-Ho,
CEO of ISU Specialty Chemical, said :
Lithium sulfide gives us a position in the solid-state supply chain. This partnership is about what sits next to it,
“Each generation we develop this way makes the next one faster, and that is the kind of capability our customers in Korea, Japan and the United States are asking us for.”
Ares Materials develops polymers and the closed-loop AI infrastructure used to formulate them against real-world performance. It has been selected for the Apple Impact Accelerator and the Amazon Climate Tech Accelerator.
Dr. David Arreaga,
CEO of Ares Materials, said :
Every materials supplier in this space knows the pattern: you hit the spec, the spec moves, and you start over,
“What we’re building with ISU is meant to break that cycle. When a model already knows how each formulation variable drives device performance, a new target is an adjustment, not a restart.”

Ampace Showcases at EICMA Milan, Redefining the Global Two-Wheeler Lithium Battery Landscape Through Reliability
— From Extreme Off-Road to Scaled Battery Swapping, Full-Scenario Solutions Demonstrate China’s Global Technology Strength
MILAN, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Ampace, a leading global provider of high-quality lithium battery solutions, is showcasing at EICMA Milan with a full-scenario portfolio for Europe and the global two-wheeler market, covering extreme off-road riding and large-scale overseas battery swapping. As two-wheeler electrification shifts from spec competition to reliability competition, Ampace’s answer is not parameter stacking but extreme-condition validation and scaled commercial data proving Chinese lithium solutions’ deployment capability.
Off-Road E-Motorcycle “Impossible Triangle”: Lightweight, Power and Fast Charging
Off-road e-motorcycles face heavy batteries, insufficient power and slow charging. Ampace transfers drone lithium-battery technology to two-wheelers and showcases JP50 and EP65 21700 cylindrical off-road cells plus custom high-energy-density pouch solutions. 9-series ultra-high-nickel cathodes with silicon-carbon anodes deliver strong performance while maintaining cycle life. Ampace’s tabless design cuts internal resistance by 80% and delivers superior thermal performance under high-current discharge. Power output remains consistent whether climbing gradients, cruising at high speed, or swinging between hot and cold temperatures, with no noticeable power fade. JP50 supports 3C+ fast charging. Both cells match European e-bike needs: long-distance capacity, fast charging, commuting and leisure. An off-road model with Ampace’s 7460 battery pack operated normally after 24-hour submersion in 3-meter-deep water.
Global Battery Swapping: Durability Proven in Complex Environments
Unlike most players still in pilots, Ampace’s swapping network has scaled commercially in China, Southeast Asia, South America and Africa. Batteries are customized for local climate, roads and operating intensity, supporting high-frequency riders in Africa’s heat and dust and Latin America’s bumpy roads. In Africa, batteries have run commercially for 2.5 years, completing 17 million swaps, with each pack averaging over 1,000 cycles under heavy, high-frequency use. Rider swapping has become a common street sight, scaling overseas.

title: Mercedes-Benz brings future technologies to life: Innovative display solutions and intelligent high-voltage battery technology in focus - Batteries News
content:
Mercedes-Benz brings future technologies to life: Innovative display solutions and intelligent high-voltage battery technology in focus
Intelligent Display in Glass: the vehicle communicates with its surroundings using LED technology
Innovative Holo Display: the windshield becomes a personalised communication surface
Pioneering Power Converter: 800-volt-capable technology with up to 3 kW output and AC charging functionality
Innovation has been at the heart of the Mercedes‑Benz DNA for 140 years. With new ideas and technologies, the company is continuously shaping automotive progress. The aim of every innovation is to offer customers genuine added value. An exclusive insight into current research and development projects underlines this ambition. The technologies contribute to the characteristic Mercedes‑Benz “Welcome home” feeling, making the vehicle even safer and more personal, information even more intuitive and the high-voltage system more efficient.
Ida Wolf
, Vice President Development Innovations, Operations & Digitalisation, Mercedes‑Benz AG, said:
The future of mobility is not created through promises, but through precision and proven engineering excellence.
“With innovations that offer clear benefits in our customers’ everyday lives, we are shaping the mobility of tomorrow – continuously, consistently and with a clear focus on the future.”
Intelligent display technology for communication and greater road safety
Safety is an essential part of the Mercedes‑Benz DNA. The company is currently working on innovative display technologies that enable a new form of communication between the vehicle and its surroundings. LED display elements are integrated directly into the vehicle windows. For example, when required, the technologies can make warning signs, safety symbols, or traffic-related information selectively visible in the rear window. When no content is displayed, the display elements laminated into the glass composite remain almost invisible, blending harmoniously into the vehicle design.
Two specialised LED technologies enable different applications. Mini LEDs are particularly suitable for larger display areas such as the rear window. They can be used, among other things, to show brake lights, warning symbols or traffic information for the road users behind. Micro LEDs, meanwhile, offer high resolution and are therefore especially suited to sophisticated visual displays on smaller display areas, such as animations. Both solutions follow the approach that content appears only when needed and otherwise remains virtually invisible.
Holographic Display: The windshield becomes an on-demand communication surface
Mercedes‑Benz is rethinking display surfaces. Instead of conventional screens, previously unused areas in the vehicle are being examined as potential information surfaces. The company is working on a holographic display that turns the windshield into a communication surface. A projector in the instrument panel projects content onto the windshield. A special transparent film laminated into the glass uses “holographic optical elements” (HOE) to selectively reflect the wavelengths of light emitted by the projector. This technology concentrates the light in such a way that the image remains visible even in sunlight. It is also visible only from specific viewing angles: the driver therefore cannot see what is shown on the passenger side – and vice versa. This opens additional information and entertainment possibilities, such as displaying context for POIs (points of interest), driving information or films. The new display is not permanently visible but shows content only when needed. This means the windshield can be used situationally for navigation, video calls, driving information or entertainment without permanently changing the vehicle’s appearance.
Innovative Power Converter: New perspectives for electric drive systems with currently up to 3 kW output for 800-volt applications
The Mercedes‑Benz Power Converter is a technology for future electric vehicles that uses programmable micro-converters to control the energy flows of individual battery cells and provide a constant high-voltage output of up to 800 volts, regardless of the cells’ state of charge or ageing. This could enable batteries and power electronics to be designed with significantly greater flexibility, efficiency and compactness in the future, while also supporting functions such as AC and DC conversion and bidirectional charging (e.g. Vehicle-to-Home or Vehicle-to-Grid). The current generation already delivers up to 3 kW of power and supports AC and DC applications.
The Power Converter thus opens new possibilities for the design of electric drive systems and charging functions in electric vehicles. The technology makes it possible to largely decouple the provision of the required high voltage from the battery architecture and instead generate it through software-controlled power electronics.
A particularly promising prospect is the modular use of the technology directly at the level of individual battery cells or cell groups. Multiple Power Converters connected in parallel regulate the energy flows individually and jointly provide a stable high-voltage DC output. This allows the overall power output to be flexibly adapted to different vehicle and system requirements. At the same time, the high-voltage output is no longer directly determined by the number of battery cells connected in series, but instead by the decentralised converters and their software-based control.
In future vehicle architectures, the Power Converter could combine several functions that are currently handled separately into a single hardware unit. The technology therefore creates new freedoms in the design of the battery and powertrain. It could improve range and efficiency and facilitate the modularisation of powertrains for battery-electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids.
Mercedes-Benz anniversary year “140 Years of Innovation”
Since Carl Benz filed the patent for the first automobile 140 years ago and Gottlieb Daimler built his motorised carriage shortly afterwards, Mercedes-Benz has dedicated itself to constant innovation and to creating the world’s most desirable cars for customers. This ambition has driven every innovation – from the world’s first automobile in 1886 to the biggest product launch programme in the company’s history that is currently underway. With its passion for performance and pioneering power, excellence and an unwavering commitment to customer service, the brand has consistently shaped the future of mobility. The result goes well beyond engineering achievement – it creates the unmistakable feeling that runs through everything Mercedes-Benz does: Welcome home.
Mercedes‑Benz is celebrating 140 years of innovation: Three new S-Class saloons went on a trans-continental journey to 140 locations worldwide as part of the “140 Years. 140 Places” tour. Each place highlighted the brand’s technology, heritage, pioneering spirit and worldwide presence. Along the way, customers, fans and colleagues got to join in the celebrations right up to its grand ‘Homecoming’ finale at the Mercedes-Benz Museum. Highlights of the tour can be found on our “
140 Years of Innovation | Mercedes‑Benz Media
” special.

LG Electronics Production Engineering Research Institute Appoints Ratel Consulting to Accelerate North American Battery Business
Ratel Consulting will support LG PRI’s North American market development, leveraging its battery industry expertise and network to expand customer opportunities for LG PRI’s turnkey battery manufacturing solutions.
SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — LG Electronics’ Production Engineering Research Institute (LG PRI) has appointed Ratel Consulting LLC as its Outside Representative for North America, effective immediately. The partnership will initially focus on the North American battery market, where LG PRI aims to expand its customer base and build new references by combining its battery manufacturing expertise with Ratel’s industry knowledge and network.
Building on its experience developing manufacturing equipment and production solutions for LG Group businesses, including home appliances, displays, semiconductors, heavy industries, automotive, pharmaceutical, LG PRI has expanded its smart factory business to external manufacturers. In batteries, LG PRI has supported more than 260 production lines worldwide, including 76 in the United States.
As a systems integrator and turnkey provider, LG PRI offers capabilities spanning electrode production, cell manufacturing, and module and pack assembly. It combines process engineering, production equipment, automation and intralogistics, supporting customers from line planning and design through installation, commissioning and production ramp-up. Drawing on these capabilities, LG PRI will prioritize module and pack manufacturing projects in its North American business development with Ratel. This targeted approach will enable LG PRI to address near-term customer needs, build regional references and progressively expand its business across the broader battery manufacturing sector.
Wonjae Hwang,
VP of Smart Factory Business Development, LG Electronics Production Engineering Research Institute, said :
Our battery manufacturing capabilities have been built through hands-on experience developing and integrating production lines.
“Through our collaboration with Ratel, we aim to bring that expertise to more North American customers and support them in translating their manufacturing plans into reliable production. Ratel’s battery industry knowledge and customer relationships will be valuable in expanding our presence in the region,”

North America is building battery and advanced manufacturing capacity at a remarkable pace.
“Often the hardest part is not building a plant but ramping it, which means hitting yield, quality, and throughput targets quickly. LG PRI has spent decades building and refining production lines including what is now the largest battery manufacturer outside of China. That experience is now available outside LG and we’re excited to help manufacturers across the region put it to work,”

LibertyStream Announces Lithium Carbonate Sales Contract with International Battery Material Maker Covering 2027–2031 Supply
DALLAS–(
BUSINESS WIRE
LibertyStream Infrastructure Partners Inc.
(TSXV: LIB | OTCQB: VLTLF | FSE: I2D) (“LibertyStream” or the “Company”) announced that it has entered into a lithium carbonate sales contract (the “Sales Contract”) with a leading international battery material maker that supplies cathodes to the U.S. market (the “Customer”). The Sales Contract provides for the Company to supply 500 metric tonnes of U.S.-origin lithium carbonate in 2027 and sets out binding terms for the supply of an additional 17,000 metric tonnes of U.S.-origin lithium carbonate through December 31, 2031, with detailed terms for 2028 through 2031 to be finalized under a separate long-term supply agreement (the “LTSA”).
Volumes for 2028 through 2031 are subject to execution of the LTSA. Pricing and other commercial terms are not being disclosed. Meeting the scheduled delivery volumes will require the Company to develop, finance and commission additional U.S. production capacity.
The Sales Contract is the definitive agreement contemplated by a memorandum of understanding between the Company and the Customer dated September 3, 2026. It follows the Company’s field operations, direct lithium extraction and refining testing, lithium carbonate production at its Freedom Launchpad facility, customer qualification programs, third-party testing and initial purchase orders.
The Sales Contract is in addition to the Company’s previously announced 600-tonne-per-year industrial offtake agreement.
Operations Update
LibertyStream continues to advance commercialization activities in support of future lithium carbonate production. LibertyStream has delivered lithium carbonate samples to multiple battery and industrial-grade prospective customers as part of ongoing product qualification and testing programs.
LibertyStream currently produces lithium carbonate from U.S. oilfield brine at its Freedom Launchpad facility in Texas. Freedom 1, located in Howard County, Texas, is the Company’s planned initial commercial facility under its previously announced agreement with Select Water Solutions. Freedom 1 is designed to integrate LibertyStream’s direct lithium extraction and refining technologies with existing oilfield water infrastructure to produce battery-grade lithium carbonate from U.S. oilfield brine.

title: New assessment tool enables comparison of costs and emissions from battery recycling technologies - Batteries News
content:
New assessment tool enables comparison of costs and emissions from battery recycling technologies
Fraunhofer FFB and the PEM Chair at RWTH Aachen University have published the “Modular Lifecycle Tool,” a computational model for evaluating recycling processes for lithium-ion batteries. The model makes it possible to compare different recycling routes under uniform assumptions regarding costs and CO₂ emissions and highlights how technological decisions along the entire recycling chain impact the overall eco-nomic and environmental balance. The model was developed as part of a consortium study with partners from the recycling, plant engineering, and consulting sectors.
As electric mobility continues to gain momentum, the recycling of lithium-ion batteries is also becoming significantly more important. Rising battery volumes, volatile raw material markets, regulatory requirements, and ambitious decarbonization targets present industry and research with the challenge of evaluating various recycling processes – under different technical and economic conditions – from both environmental and economic perspectives.
To systematically compare different recycling concepts, the Fraunhofer Research Institution for Battery Cell Production FFB and the Chair of Production Engineering of E-Mobility Components (PEM) at RWTH Aachen University, in collaboration with industry partners, have developed a modular life-cycle approach for evaluating battery recycling processes.
The “Modular Lifecycle Tool,” developed by Fraunhofer FFB and the PEM Chair at RWTH Aachen University, makes it possible to compare different recycling processes for lithium-ion batteries in terms of costs and CO₂ emissions on a uniform basis.
Comparability Through a Modular Structure
A particular challenge in evaluating battery recycling processes is that the various methods have different process structures, energy requirements, recovery rates, and costs. Furthermore, decisions made in early process steps influence material quality, recovery rates, and the effort required in downstream stages.
The “Modular Lifecycle Tool” therefore does not consider individual technologies in isolation but rather maps out the entire recycling chain using a modular principle. The process chain is first divided into the areas of preparation and pretreatment of the recycling material, as well as material recovery. Within these areas, distinctions are made between functions, process steps, and specific technologies.
“The modular structure allows us to compare different technologies within the same process logic,” explains Lucca Groß, a research assistant at the Chair of “Production Engineering of E-Mobility Components (PEM)” at RWTH Aachen University. “For example, the shredding process step can be implemented using various shredder technologies. The different technologies can be specifically swapped out in the model, making it immediately apparent how a technological change affects the entire recycling chain.”
Costs, Material Flows, and Emissions in a Single Model
At the heart of the approach is a database of individual process steps. Users can configure the input stream of a recycling chain – including throughput and material composition – and then assemble customized process chains. The model tracks material flows throughout the entire recycling chain and links them to economic and environmental metrics. Factors taken into account include energy requirements and associated emissions, consumables and auxiliary materials, operating expenses, investment-related costs, revenues from recovered materials, and disposal costs. Site-specific factors such as the electricity mix and labor costs, as well as capacity utilization and economies of scale, can also be incorporated into the analysis.
This does not result in a static cost table, but rather a dynamic evaluation environment for the overall economic balance. If, for example, separation efficiency, throughput, or recovery intensity change, the effects on downstream material flows, costs, revenues, and emissions become apparent.
A Foundation for Investment and Technology Decisions
“With this tool, we aim to make different recycling concepts comparable on a common basis and thereby create a robust foundation for technological and strategic decisions. In this way, the tool supports recycling companies in optimizing existing processes, technology providers in evaluating new solutions, and battery manufacturers in comparing different recycling strategies,” says Benedikt Gruber, research associate at Fraunhofer FFB.
Possible applications include:
Comparison of alternative recycling concepts within uniform system boundaries
Identification of cost and emissions hotspots along the process chain
Evaluation of scaling strategies and scenarios for industrial ramp-up
Evaluation of site-specific conditions, including energy supply
Sensitivity analysis of key technical and economic parameters
In the future, the evaluation framework can be expanded to include additional battery chemistries, more regionally differentiated datasets, and future regulatory scenarios.

Industry lobby groups praise lower automotive supply chain CO2 targets, balancing European climate goals while promoting green steel and EU EV assembly
Members of an influential European Parliament sub-committee voted to reduce proposed automotive emission reduction targets, while easing corporate fleet targets, which will ease requirements for automakers to sell zero-emission vehicles by 2035.
New categories to support EU EV production
The proposal included the introduction of a new category of small sized electric vehicle (EV), and introduced categories of “highly efficient EVs” and “zero emission vans” for EU-made passenger vehicles and vans, respectively. The three categories would be expected to receive targeted support mechanisms to boost sales of EU-manufactured vehicles in these segments.
The revisions include expanding the scope of the super-credits mechanism for European auto manufacturers.
Market penetration from Chinese carmakers
EU manufacturers have struggled to compete against imports of competitively-priced EVs from Asian manufacturers, with market penetration in smaller categories leading to loss of market share, industry analysts note.
In October 2026, the EU's trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, reached an agreement with China to limit exports of low cost battery hybrid electric vehicles (BHEV) into the EU. Exports from Chinese automakers have risen, with overall Chinese vehicles accounting for 12% of overall European sales in August 2026, according to Dataforce. China now accounts for 34% of plug-in BHEV sales, with major Chinese BHEV exporters including BYD, Chery, MG and Geely taking a larger share of the European market.
The introduction of a green steel premium for automobiles assembled using EU steel would benefit steelmakers such as ArcelorMittal, which has invested in its Dunkirk plant (Credit: ArcelorMittal)
We fought against the combustion engine ban from the very beginning, and today we have secured the majority to deliver. The EPP Group managed to bring Europe’s political centre together behind a clear objective: backing our car industry, protecting European jobs and giving manufacturers the freedom to develop the best technologies
Massimiliano Salini MEP, the European Parliament’s rapporteur on vehicle decarbonisation

China now accounts for 34% of plug-in BHEV sales, with major Chinese BHEV exporters including BYD, Chery, MG and Geely taking a larger share of the European market.
The European Commission has watered down its commitment to phasing out internal combustion engines vehicles.
Green steel premium
The three mainstream parties reached an agreement to reduce emissions from internal combustion engines by 87.5%, compared with a 90% reduction proposed by the European Commission in late 2025.
However, the measures were noteworthy for the introduction of a 7.5% premium for automakers using low-carbon steel from producers located in the EU.
This was welcomed by Peter Liese MEP (CDU/EPP), member of the Committee for Environment and Climate in the European Parliament and climate policy spokesperson for the EPP Group, the largest political group in the European Parliament. “I am particularly pleased that we have given climate-friendly steel a special role. European steelmakers were understandably upbeat about the vote. “Europe’s steelmakers are investing to produce low-carbon steel but what is the point of transforming our plants if there is no market for the steel they produce? This steel credit can turn demand from European carmakers into investment, production and quality jobs in Europe. Low-carbon steel made in the EU should go into cars made in the EU,” Axel Eggert, Director-General of EUROFER, commented.
However, the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) struck a more cautious note, warning that “the agreed text includes some additional flexibility, but for passenger cars this remains too limited in scope and duration to adequately address the industry’s concerns.”
Crude steel production at an electric arc furnace at a steel mill. [Getty]
Key facts
Revised 2035 Mandates: The committee proposes to amend the 2035 CO2 emission reduction target from the European Commission's 90% reduction to a 87.5% reduction requirement.
Green Steel Credits: Automakers can secure an additional 7.5% compliance credit by integrating European-made green steel into their manufacturing supply chain.
Green steel projects: The steel credit mechanism will create an end-user market to support major investments in steelmaking hubs such as thyssenkrupp's Duisburg (Germany), ArcelorMittal Dunkirk (France), Stegra in Boden (Sweden) and Taranto (Italy).
E-Fuel Compatibility: Plug-in hybrids with extended ranges running on climate-neutral synthetic fuels will remain fully compliant with 2035 climate goals.
The proposal included the introduction of a new category of small sized electric vehicle (EV), and introduced categories of “highly efficient EVs” and “zero emission vans” for EU-made passenger vehicles and vans, respectively.
Automated driving regulations
Among the committee's other recommendations, ENVI proposed that the European Commission adopt technical requirements by 31 December 2027 to ensure the interoperability of EVs and plug-in BHEVs with charging infrastructure.
Looking further ahead, the committee also recommended that national authorisations for the testing and deployment of automated vehicles be mutually recognised, as a step to facilitating the introduction of automated vehicles. The European Commission will also be expected to introduce harmonised minimum requirements to support the introduction of the rapidly evolving technology.
Next steps
The vote within the Environment committee needs to be approved by the European Parliament as a whole before it is adopted by the parliament as a negotiating position. Once put to the vote in December and potentially adopted, the parliament's negotiators will discuss the issue with the members of the European Council, which includes ministerial representatives from the EU's member states.
If adopted, it would represent a further step away from the previously expected complete cessation of ICE vehicle sales in 2035.

Prioritise Us
