title: Unmanned underwater vehicle hunts and neutralizes naval mines
content: An autonomous underwater vehicle has completed an end-to-end mine countermeasure demonstration, bringing naval forces closer to safer and faster mine-clearing operations. The exercise connected underwater search, sonar-based identification, and mine neutralization within one coordinated mission.HII and Thales conducted the demonstration using an integrated network of autonomous underwater systems and specialized mine-countermeasure equipment. The setup centered on HII’s REMUS 620 unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) and Thales’ Expeditionary PathMaster architecture.The system followed a complete Find, Fix, Finish workflow. It allowed operators to detect potential mine threats and coordinate their identification and subsequent neutralization. The approach also reduces the need to send crewed platforms close to suspected minefields.Autonomous systems hunt minesNaval mines remain a persistent threat to maritime operations. They can restrict shipping routes, disrupt commercial traffic, and force warships to avoid entire areas. Traditional mine-clearing missions often involve several platforms and repeated deployments before operators can confirm a threat.The integrated system aims to shorten that process. Its REMUS 620 UUV carries Thales’ SAMDIS 600 multi-aspect sonar to scan the underwater environment for potential mines. HII’s command-and-control software manages the vehicle and connects its operations with Thales’ Expeditionary Portable Operation Center (ePOC).The ePOC serves as the mission’s central control hub. It hosts Thales’ mission management system and sonar analysis software alongside HII’s Odyssey mission management solution. Operators can monitor mission assets through a unified operational picture.Once the sonar detects suspicious objects, Thales’ software analyzes the collected imagery. Its Automatic Target Recognition technology helps operators classify and pinpoint mine-like objects. Human personnel retain oversight of the identification process and subsequent operational decisions.Finding and neutralizing threatsThe demonstration’s final phase brought in Thales Advanced Acoustic Concepts’ ANGLER underwater effector. An accompanying remotely operated vehicle (ROV) rapidly reacquired the previously detected objects. It then conducted visual inspections to establish whether they represented mine threats.The ANGLER system provides the means to engage and neutralize identified mines. This completes the mission chain without requiring sailors to approach suspected explosives directly.The exercise also tested automated launch and recovery capabilities. HII’s Sea Launcher system deployed and recovered the REMUS 620, which carried the SAMDIS 600 sonar. This adds another layer of automation to expeditionary mine warfare operations.Thales’ open Expeditionary PathMaster architecture also supports equipment from multiple manufacturers. Its NATO-compliant framework allows allied navies to combine different autonomous vehicles, sensors and neutralization systems. This could make it easier to adapt mine-clearing capabilities across different naval fleets.Faster mine countermeasure missionsThe demonstration expands on a 2025 integration exercise involving the SAMDIS 600 sonar and REMUS 620. That earlier work focused on sensor integration and underwater performance. The newer exercise incorporated mission management, automated target recognition, and mine neutralization.“Together, we are giving naval forces a path to conduct these demanding missions faster, at greater scale and with sailors farther from the mine threat,” said Duane Fotheringham, president of HII’s Unmanned Systems group.Sébastien Guérémy, Thales‘ vice president of Underwater Systems, said the exercise demonstrated how different autonomous platforms and specialized equipment could operate within one framework.The approach could help US and allied navies reduce personnel exposure during dangerous mine-clearing missions. It also offers a more flexible way to deploy underwater systems across expeditionary operations.

title: MIT puts next-generation stellarator magnet through full-force test
content: Thea Energy has partnered with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) to test a full-scale superconducting magnet designed for its next-generation stellarator, marking another step in the company’s effort to develop a commercial fusion power plant by 2035.The collaboration will see Thea Energy and MIT’s Plasma Science and Fusion Center (PSFC) test a full-field, full-force planar encircling coil for the company’s Eos stellarator. The tests will assess whether the magnet can withstand the intense magnetic fields and mechanical forces expected during power-plant operation.The work will use MIT’s cryogenic testing facilities and its expertise in high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets. The partners will also examine the coil’s efficiency under power-plant-relevant conditions and develop predictive models to assess its performance.Stellarators use magnetic fields to confine superheated plasma, the electrically charged gas in which fusion reactions take place. Their magnets must maintain precise field configurations while withstanding substantial mechanical stresses.Traditional stellarator magnets have complex three-dimensional shapes, making them difficult and expensive to manufacture. Thea Energy is pursuing a different approach with a planar-coil architecture intended to simplify magnet production, construction and maintenance.Flat coils simplify constructionThe company’s Eos design uses 12 encircling coils alongside approximately 300 programmable shaping magnets. The encircling coils generate the magnetic field needed to confine the plasma, while the smaller shaping magnets fine-tune its configuration.The modular shaping magnets can be adjusted in strength and replaced individually to account for variations during assembly, as well as wear and tear during operation. Thea Energy says it has already built and validated these shaping coils at full scale.The encircling coil is the next major component being put through testing. Evaluating it at full magnetic field and full mechanical force is intended to establish whether the design can meet the demanding requirements of a commercial fusion system.The partners will also test the magnet’s resilience to help determine its reliability and support high plant availability. These factors are important because a commercial fusion facility would need to operate consistently rather than simply demonstrate that it can produce a fusion reaction.Testing supports commercial ambitionsThea Energy says the collaboration will help de-risk key engineering milestones on its path to commercial fusion by 2035. It follows the company’s work with national laboratories, academic institutions and industrial partners to develop its stellarator architecture.The company’s subsequent power-plant design, Helios, will use the same planar-coil approach, incorporating both encircling and shaping magnets. Thea Energy aims to use this shared architecture to reduce manufacturing complexity and make large-scale deployment more practical.The partnership also builds on a broader effort to use modelling and simulation to accelerate fusion development. Thea Energy has previously announced a collaboration involving NVIDIA, Synopsys, Argonne National Laboratory and Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory to develop a digital twin of its Helios power plant.However, the MIT collaboration focuses on physical testing of the encircling magnet, providing data on how the component performs under demanding operating conditions.Thea Energy was spun out of Princeton University and Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory in 2022 to commercialize its stellarator technology. Its latest collaboration with MIT aims to turn the simplified magnet architecture into a system capable of supporting a future fusion power plant.

title: Sentinel's 15,000-mph ICBM reentry vehicle passes crucial flight test
content: Lockheed Martin has completed another flight test of a next-generation reentry vehicle designed for America’s future nuclear-armed intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs). The unarmed Mk21A flew over the Pacific Ocean after launching from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. The test advances development of a critical component for the U.S. Air Force’s upcoming LGM-35A Sentinel missile.Sentinel will eventually replace the Minuteman III, which has served as America’s land-based nuclear deterrent since 1970. The new missile will reach approximately 15,000 mph at burnout, according to the Air Force. Its reentry vehicle must protect its payload as it travels through space and plunges back into Earth’s atmosphere at extreme speeds.Testing a critical componentThe Mk21A serves as the front-end payload section of the Sentinel ICBM. Lockheed Martin is developing it to house the W87-1 nuclear warhead. Its structure must withstand the intense thermal and mechanical stresses associated with atmospheric reentry.Unlike a complete missile flight, this test focused on the developmental reentry vehicle. The Air Force and Lockheed Martin used the flight to assess its architecture and validate technologies intended for future operational missions. The vehicle carried no nuclear warhead during the demonstration.The Mk21A builds on the design of the older Mk21 reentry vehicle. However, its upgraded configuration must accommodate the W87-1 warhead and meet Sentinel’s requirements. The vehicle also incorporates specialized electronics and systems that support payload delivery and weapon safety.The Air Force plans to replace its existing fleet of Minuteman III missiles with Sentinel. Northrop Grumman leads development of the three-stage solid-fuel missile, while Lockheed Martin handles its next-generation reentry vehicle.Surviving extreme reentry speedsSentinel’s projected burnout speed of approximately 15,000 mph illustrates the demanding environment surrounding its payload. The missile accelerates through multiple rocket stages before releasing its payload toward its intended trajectory. The reentry vehicle must then protect the warhead as it returns through the atmosphere.Extreme aerodynamic heating makes thermal protection particularly important. The vehicle’s heat shield must withstand intense temperatures without compromising the structure or its protected payload. Its electronics must also remain functional throughout the demanding flight environment.Lockheed Martin is using high-fidelity simulations and digital engineering to accelerate development. Engineers combine modeling with data collected during earlier flight tests. Results from the latest demonstration will guide design changes and help shape subsequent testing.Sentinel faces development challengesThe Mk21A program operates under a military contract worth more than $1 billion. Its next major milestone involves a system-level Critical Design Review. Testing data will help engineers establish whether the vehicle meets its required performance specifications.Jason Watson, Lockheed Martin’s vice president of Strategic Reentry Programs, described testing as essential to improving reliability. He said engineers are translating previous flight experience into progress across the program.Sentinel itself faces a more complicated development schedule. The program has encountered substantial cost growth and delays, prompting the Pentagon to restructure its development approach. The Government Accountability Office has highlighted these challenges as the Air Force works toward replacing its aging ICBM fleet.The Mk21A’s progress therefore represents an important step within a much larger modernization effort. Its successful development will help determine whether Sentinel can deliver the next generation of America’s land-based nuclear deterrent.

title: OpenAI agents expose 948 Linux flaws with 10 new attack methods-63
content: OpenAI has developed an automated cybersecurity research pipeline that identified 948 distinct Linux kernel vulnerabilities capable of allowing local users to gain root access, while uncovering at least 10 previously undocumented exploitation techniques.The system analyzed thousands of potential security issues, reproduced vulnerabilities in controlled environments and generated working exploits and candidate patches for human review.In a research post, OpenAI said the pipeline identified 2,308 candidate findings and dynamically reproduced 1,724 of them. It subsequently generated 1,169 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits, which variant analysis narrowed to 948 distinct vulnerabilities.The mid-October 2026 campaign used an upcoming cyber model that the company has not yet publicly identified. The full run cost $1.21 million in API credits, averaging about $1,279 per distinct LPE vulnerability.The research highlights how increasingly capable models could help security teams identify and fix flaws in critical software before attackers exploit them.Automated security pipelineOpenAI’s system followed a five-stage process covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, patch generation and human review.Scout agents first identified security-relevant sections of the Linux kernel, narrowing the audit to 5,034 targets covering about 2.8 million lines of code, or roughly 7 percent of the codebase.Our security researchers built an autonomous cyber vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching pipeline.In a single run with an upcoming cyber model, it validated and generated patches for 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel at a total API… pic.twitter.com/Nu2I0n2ayI— OpenAI (@OpenAI) November 4, 2026Analyst agents then examined those targets and produced 2,308 candidate findings within 12 hours. The system attempted to reproduce each issue inside isolated virtual machines, confirming 1,724 vulnerabilities within 30 hours.Exploit-development agents tested whether the validated flaws could expose information or enable local privilege escalation. The system produced 291 information-leak proofs of concept and 1,169 working LPE exploits.Variant analysis identified 948 distinct vulnerabilities behind those exploits. The pipeline also generated candidate patches, with human security researchers reviewing the findings before they were reported to maintainers.OpenAI said it had already sent hundreds of reports and patches for critical vulnerabilities, following guidance from the Linux kernel community. It is working with Patch the Planet partners to report and address additional issues.New exploitation methodsThe researchers sampled 166 exploits and found that the agents had used at least 10 exploitation techniques that, to their knowledge, were previously undocumented. Third-party kernel exploitation experts consulted by the team also considered the techniques new.These included methods for placing objects inside kernel memory caches, improving exploit reliability and obtaining privilege escalation through data-only attacks.The newer pipeline also showed a substantial increase over an earlier campaign. In July 2026, GPT-5.6 Sol found and exploited 166 unique LPE vulnerabilities at a cost of $513,690. The October run identified 948, more than five times as many, despite three months of additional kernel hardening.OpenAI compared the 948 vulnerabilities with historical Linux kernel bug bounty payouts from Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN. Applying those past rewards produced a hypothetical valuation of $18.9 million to $66.3 million, or 16 to 55 times the pipeline’s cost. This is an illustrative comparison, not actual bounty income.The company said its goal is to help defenders discover and fix vulnerabilities before attackers can use them. It also stressed that automated patch generation and repeated security reviews will be important as model capabilities improve.The findings were published by OpenAI as part of its Patch the Planet initiative.

title: Rovers could deploy a 100 kW power network across the lunar surface
content: Astrolab plans to build a lunar power and communications network capable of delivering more than 100 kilowatts (kW) of electricity using utility nodes deployed by its FLEX rovers.The company unveiled the Lunar Utility Module for Industrial Services (LUMIS) on November 4, describing it as a system designed to provide energy, connectivity, and data services to customers operating on the Moon.Initial LUMIS demonstration nodes are designed to generate 2 kW of power each, while future versions could reach 20 kW. Multiple units could be delivered on a cargo lander, transported by a single FLEX rover and connected to form a network exceeding 100 kW.Astrolab says this approach could provide substantial power before anticipated nuclear energy systems become available, without the regulatory and safety requirements associated with nuclear installations.The announcement also marks the expansion of Astrolab’s business beyond lunar rovers. Its newly introduced Lunar Operating System (LUNAR OS) combines FLEX mobility systems with LUMIS power, communications and data services to support longer-term human and robotic operations.Rovers position lunar infrastructureUnlike conventional infrastructure delivered to a fixed landing site, LUMIS nodes could be transported tens of kilometers across the lunar surface after landing.Astrolab’s FLEX rover would carry the equipment to locations with better sunlight exposure and communications coverage. This separates the choice of a safe landing location from the positioning of operational infrastructure, potentially allowing more equipment to be delivered with fewer lunar flights.The distinction is particularly important near the Moon’s south pole, where small changes in terrain can affect solar exposure and direct visibility of Earth.Astrolab said moving infrastructure by just 50 meters could result in hundreds of additional hours of darkness or reduce near-continuous visibility of Earth to roughly half the time.The company identified the Shackleton–de Gerlache connecting ridge as an area where communications coverage could be challenging. LUMIS nodes positioned at elevated locations on Malapert Massif or Mons Mouton could maintain near-continuous links with Earth while retaining visibility of the ridge, more than 100 kilometers away.Nodes placed along the ridge could then relay communications through inter-node links, providing local Wi-Fi and 5G connectivity for equipment and operations.Power supports sustained operationsLUMIS is being developed with a vertical solar array tower, batteries, transceivers, wireless power transfer capabilities, and onboard edge computing.The system is designed to provide direct-to-Earth communications, local wireless connectivity and long-range backhaul links between installations. Its internal power reserves are intended to support operations for more than 400 hours while continuing to supply external payloads.Potential applications include recharging visiting rovers, transmitting scientific data to Earth and powering equipment used for in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), which involves extracting and processing local lunar materials.Astrolab plans to offer these capabilities as services through LUNAR OS. Rather than building and maintaining their own infrastructure, customers could pay for access and usage, with shared facilities for smaller users and dedicated equipment for larger requirements.The company is targeting its first LUMIS deployment in 2028 as part of its previously announced commercial FLEX mission aboard SpaceX’s Starship.Astrolab was previously selected to develop a crewed lunar rover for NASA’s Artemis program. It is also preparing its FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) for a planned launch aboard Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 lander as part of a NASA lunar south pole mission.

title: Anthropic maps world's first 3D vault built from 96 protein copies
content: Scientists have mapped the first three-dimensional structure of a vault particle linked to bacterial life, uncovering a previously unexplored branch of these mysterious protein assemblies. The discovery could give researchers a simpler way to investigate structures found in human cells. Anthropic’s biology research team used Claude throughout the investigation, from identifying promising proteins to reconstructing their molecular architecture.Vault particles have puzzled biologists for nearly four decades. Despite their enormous size and widespread presence in complex organisms, researchers still cannot explain their biological purpose. The new findings reveal that related proteins can assemble into similar structures in bacteria and bacteriophages. This discovery could help scientists trace their evolutionary history and understand their role in living cells.Mystery across lifeLeonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha first identified vault particles in 1986. These hollow, barrel-shaped structures rank among the largest protein complexes found in human cells. Mammalian vaults contain 78 copies of a major protein arranged into two symmetrical halves.Their biological purpose remains uncertain despite decades of investigation. Researchers have proposed roles in cellular transport, drug resistance, and immune defense. However, experiments have yet to establish any of these functions conclusively.The structures also appear across much of the evolutionary tree. Their presence in organisms ranging from slime molds to humans suggests an important biological role. However, researchers have struggled to investigate them because common laboratory organisms lack vaults.We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were…— Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) November 4, 2026Anthropic’s team searched approximately 15 billion predicted protein sequences for distant relatives. The search identified potential vault proteins across 29 major bacterial groups and four groups of archaea. The researchers selected 44 candidates for laboratory testing.Inside the bacterial vaultExperiments revealed that seven of the 15 successfully produced proteins assembled into vault-like particles. Cryogenic electron microscopy, or cryo-EM, confirmed the structures of four candidates. Two came from bacteria, while the other two originated from bacteriophages.The researchers selected a phage-derived protein called L05 for detailed structural analysis. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria and use their cellular machinery. The L05 protein assembled into a complete structure containing 96 copies of itself.The resulting particle measures approximately 54 nanometers long and 45 nanometers wide. Its combined molecular mass reaches roughly 9.5 megadaltons. Despite its shorter length, the structure encloses approximately 25 percent more volume than mammalian vaults.Researchers also modified the protein to investigate how these structures grow. Adding two repeating segments produced an even larger particle. Its enclosed volume increased by approximately 20 percent.These experiments suggest protein duplication could have helped vaults evolve different sizes. They also revealed how small structural changes can prevent particles from closing properly.Claude accelerates discoveryClaude contributed throughout the research process, including protein searches, DNA design, purification, and microscopy analysis. One major breakthrough involved simplifying the particle isolation process.Traditional purification methods take approximately three days. The team developed a chromatography-based approach that reduced the process to roughly 90 minutes. Claude helped identify suitable equipment and optimize the experimental procedure.The researchers also used Claude to process cryo-EM data. Their first complete structural model emerged within 34 hours. The team estimates conventional analysis could require several weeks.However, the project exposed limitations alongside those gains. One experimental protocol introduced an additive that interfered with DNA delivery. That mistake delayed the research by two weeks. Claude also produced an inaccurate structural map after skipping a standard processing step.The researchers eventually corrected these problems through closer supervision. They also shared laboratory observations with Claude’s development team to improve future performance.Despite the structural breakthrough, the central mystery remains unsolved. Researchers have yet to determine what vault particles actually do inside living organisms. Leonard Rome, one of their original discoverers, described the question as enormously challenging. The new findings provide another route toward answering it, but much of the biology remains unexplored.

title: Drone turned into weapon carrier, integrates kamikaze UAVs that hit targets
content: A Turkish defense technology company has taken a significant step to expand capabilities of its unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs). Bayraktar has tested its TB2 drone carrying 16 Skydagger FPV kamikaze UAVs. During a test flight conducted with Skydagger FPV kamikaze drones, Bayraktar TB2 struck designated targets with pinpoint accuracy using two air-launched FPV drones.Bayraktar TB2 drone struck a designated target with pinpoint accuracyDeveloped indigenously by Baykar, the TB2 UCAV (Unmanned Combat Aerial Vehicle) continues to be reinforced with new capabilities tailored to the evolving conditions of the battlefield. In the latest test conducted, Bayraktar TB2 struck a designated target with pinpoint accuracy using FPV kamikaze drones developed by Skydagger.The company revealed that the Bayraktar TB2 took off from the Keşan Flight Training and Test Center carrying 16 Skydagger FPV kamikaze drones and transited to the test site. At the test site, two FPV drones were released from Bayraktar TB2. Through the connection established via Bayraktar TB2, the drones — controlled by operators independent of the ground — struck the designated targets with pinpoint accuracy.World’s largest exporter in drone segmentHaving carried out all of its projects entirely with its own resources from the outset, Baykar remained the world’s largest exporter in the unmanned aerial vehicle segment in 2025 as well. Having sustained its leadership in the global UCAV market over the past three years, Baykar renewed its own record with an export volume of $2.2 billion reached in 2025. Deriving 90% of its revenue from exports in recent years, Baykar has become the locomotive of Türkiye’s high-technology exports, according to a press release.The integration of FPV drones with larger unmanned combat aircraft reflects the continuing evolution of modern military aviation. FPV drones have attracted considerable attention in contemporary conflicts because of their relatively compact size and ability to be operated remotely, as per the release.Combining these smaller platforms with a larger UCAV introduces the possibility of deploying multiple unmanned systems from a single airborne platform. It also highlights the growing importance of interoperability between different categories of unmanned aircraft.Future developments in this field are likely to place greater emphasis on interoperability, autonomous coordination, secure communications and the ability to operate multiple unmanned platforms within a common operational framework.The drone’s latest demonstration underlines how the future of military aviation is increasingly being shaped by the integration of larger unmanned aircraft with smaller, specialised aerial systems.The test involved the integration of the Bayraktar TB2 with Skydagger FPV kamikaze drones. The demonstration showcased the potential of combining a larger unmanned aerial platform with smaller, independently operated aerial systems.The test represents an important development in the integration of different classes of unmanned aerial systems. Rather than operating exclusively as a conventional surveillance and strike platform, the Bayraktar TB2 demonstrated its ability to serve as an airborne carrier for smaller unmanned systems.

title: PUDU displays 22-lb-lifting semi-humanoid, all-terrain LiDAR robot dog
content: Chinese robotics giant PUDU Robotics showcased all six of its robot product lines together for the first time at its European Partner Summit, including the D7 semi-humanoid robot with an eight-hour runtime, the Nvidia-powered D5 robot dog, and the cat-inspired BellaBot Pro service robot.The summit took place at the Van der Valk Amsterdam-Amstel in the Netherlands, on Wednesday, November 4. During the event, the Shenzhen-based firm unveiled its new “One Brain, Multiple Embodiments” strategy.Felix Zhang, PUDU Robotics’ founder and CEO, said the strategy will use the same artificial intelligence (AI) technology across all of its products. He said that robots must become smarter, easier to deploy, and cheaper to achieve wider adoption.“With our ‘One Brain, Multiple Embodiments’ strategy, we are building a shared technological foundation across different robot forms – from specialized service robots to semi-humanoid and humanoid robots,” Zhang said. In the spotlightThe PUDU D7, a semi-humanoid robot that relies on wheels to move and human-like arms to handle objects, was a crowd favorite at the event. First introduced in September 2024, the robot is 5.4 feet (1.65 meters) tall and weighs about 99 lbs (45 kilograms). It can operate continuously for more than eight hours on a battery exceeding one kilowatt-hour (kWh). At the same time, it features 30 degrees of freedom, which can raise to 50 with a dexterous hand attachment. Its robotic arms can lift up to 22 lbs, while its wheels allow it to move in any direction. It can transport objects, sort items, and even use elevators in workplaces such as offices, warehouses, and factories. Service robots on display at the European Partner Summit in Amsterdam.Credit: PUDU RoboticsPUDU also showcased the D5 and D5-W quadruped robots, which are equipped with an Nvidia Jetson Orin AGX processor and an RK3588 chip. The robot dogs use two LiDAR sensors and four fisheye cameras to spot obstacles and navigate their surroundings. The company underscored that they can deliver up to 275 trillion operations per second (TOPS) of computing performance. Both models can climb slopes of up to 45 degrees and carry between 44 and 66 lbs (20 and 30 kilograms) while walking.The BellaBot Pro, a cat-like delivery robot, with an interactive screen that displays playful facial expressions, was also among the highlights. Built for restaurants and other commercial spaces, it delivers food and interacts with customers.A diverse robotics lineupThe company also displayed more machines for workplaces, factories, and homes, including the CC1 PRO, which can sweep, scrub, vacuum, and mop floors. Also, for industrial purposes, it exhibited the MP2000, an autonomous robot that can carry pallets weighing up to 4,409 lbs (2,000 kilograms) and insert its forks into them in just 20 seconds.PUDU also introduced its outdoor robots, including the GT series for businesses and TOMO S series for homeowners. Made for home lawn care, this is the firm’s first consumer robotics product. Robots on display at the European Partner Summit in Amsterdam.Credit: PUDU RoboticsThe expanded lineup also reflects PUDU’s ambitions to strengthen its presence in Europe. Bella Sun, PUDU Robotics VP and GM for Europe, shared with Interesting Engineering (IE) that the company wants Europe to be among the first markets to adopt its new strategy. “We see huge potential in the European market,” Sun told IE. “The direction is pretty clear. Customers across Europe are becoming more open to robotics technology.”At the same time, Zhang also stressed that the goal is to support human workers rather than replace them. He also addressed the company’s future in the US amid new restrictions affecting Chinese robotics products.“The FCC regulation is only for new products, meaning all of our existing products can be sold in the US,” he concluded. “[But] I want our robots working everywhere in the world.”

title: 4.95-MW US agrivoltaic solar farm to offer 10% cheaper electricity
content: A 4.95-megawatt (MW) agrivoltaic solar project has secured approval in Illinois, paving the way for a community solar facility that will continue producing hay while generating renewable electricity.According to a press statement, the Paxton City Council Tuesday (November 3) approved an annexation agreement for the Baltimore Drive Solar Project, allowing the roughly 35-acre site to become part of the city and enabling property tax revenue from the development to flow directly to Paxton. Residents, businesses, and public institutions subscribing to the community solar project are expected to save about 10% on their electricity bills, the statement said.Unlike conventional solar farms that often remove farmland from production, the project has been designed as an agrivoltaic installation, allowing crops to grow beneath and between rows of solar panels.Solar panels, hay to share same landDeveloped by Lightstar Renewables, a Boston-based solar energy company, the project will occupy around 30 acres of leased agricultural land while preserving hay production throughout the site’s operational life.The facility will use single-axis solar trackers, which rotate throughout the day to follow the sun and increase electricity generation compared with fixed-tilt panels. The trackers will stand up to 12 feet (3.7 meters) high, leaving enough clearance for agricultural machinery to continue cutting and baling hay beneath the arrays.The site will also be enclosed with livestock-style fencing designed to blend into the surrounding agricultural landscape.Unlike many modern utility-scale solar facilities, the Baltimore Drive project will not include battery energy storage. Instead, electricity generated by the installation will flow directly into the local distribution grid through an existing grid interconnection selected for its capacity and proximity.The company said the project builds on experience gained from New York’s first permitted agrivoltaics installation at DiMartino Farm, where hay continues to be harvested alongside solar panels.Community solar with local benefitsThe project will participate in Illinois’ community solar program, allowing households, businesses, and public entities to subscribe without installing rooftop solar panels. Subscribers receive bill credits based on their share of the project’s electricity output, with expected savings of approximately 10 percent on electricity costs.The agreement also creates long-term financial benefits for the city.According to the developer, the project will support city revenues for decades while placing little additional demand on municipal infrastructure such as water, sewer, and schools. A separate community benefits agreement will provide additional financial contributions to Paxton.Last October, Baltimore County, Maryland, switched on its first large-scale ground-mounted solar farm, transforming the former Parkton Landfill into a hub of clean energy generation.The 7-megawatt installation spanned more than 213 acres and featured four solar arrays with nearly 15,000 ground-mounted photovoltaic panels. In its first year alone, the site was expected to generate around 8.2 million kilowatt-hours of electricity—enough to supply roughly 11 percent of the county government’s annual power needs, according to a report.The recent project in Illinois demonstrates how agrivoltaics can combine renewable power generation with continued agricultural production, allowing farmland to deliver both crops and clean energy from the same acreage.​

title: SpaceX taps Qualcomm as Starlink prepares a huge nationwide 5G push
content: SpaceX plans to build a nationwide terrestrial 5G network in the U.S. for its Starlink Mobile service, deploying tens of thousands of base stations from 2027 through a new collaboration with Qualcomm.The Elon-Musk led space transportation company has picked Qualcomm’s Dragonwing cellular infrastructure platforms to support the network.. The technology will combine high-capacity radio and baseband processing with power-efficient computing to support large-scale cellular deployments.Under the multi-year agreement, Qualcomm will supply its Dragonwing QRU100 and QDU100 platforms, along with commercial-grade Layer 1 software for SpaceX’s planned nationwide terrestrial wireless network. The collaboration will support SpaceX’s development of an end-to-end base station architecture for its terrestrial network.The move expands SpaceX’s connectivity strategy beyond its satellite constellation. Starlink Mobile plans to combine terrestrial cellular infrastructure with satellite connectivity to provide a more integrated network for users across the US.Massive MIMO boosts capacityA key component of the planned network is Massive Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) technology, which uses multiple transmitters and receivers to improve wireless communication.Starlink Mobile will deploy radio units with 64 transmit and 64 receive paths, known as 64T64R. The configuration is designed to improve network coverage, increase capacity and make more efficient use of available radio spectrum.Massive MIMO uses multiple antenna elements to direct radio signals towards users, rather than broadcasting them uniformly in every direction. This technique, known as beamforming, can help networks serve more users and handle greater data traffic within a given area.SpaceX has selected Qualcomm #Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure solutions to support @Starlink Mobile’s nationwide terrestrial 5G network in the U.S. https://t.co/Up7LxbQz5o— Qualcomm (@Qualcomm) November 4, 2026Qualcomm’s QRU100 platform will provide integrated processing for the Massive MIMO radio units. Its QDU100 platform will handle Layer 1 processing, which manages the physical transmission and reception of data over cellular networks.The two platforms are designed to improve performance per watt across radio and distributed-unit processing. This could help reduce the energy requirements and operating costs associated with deploying and running thousands of cellular base stations.Network targets 2027 rolloutSpaceX plans to begin the nationwide deployment in 2027, with tens of thousands of sites expected to be installed over the multi-year agreement. The companies have not disclosed the financial terms of their collaboration.The planned infrastructure will complement Starlink’s satellite network, which provides connectivity in areas where conventional terrestrial networks have limited reach. Ground-based cellular stations could help deliver additional coverage and capacity, particularly in populated areas where satellite connectivity alone may not meet demand.The announcement also marks a commercial step towards Qualcomm and SpaceX’s longer-term vision for AI-native sixth-generation (6G) wireless infrastructure.Although the initial deployment will focus on 5G, Qualcomm said the platforms offer an adaptable foundation for future connectivity technologies and more intelligent network operations.For SpaceX, the partnership provides access to specialized radio and baseband technology as it develops its terrestrial network. For Qualcomm, the deal expands its role beyond mobile-device processors into large-scale telecommunications infrastructure.The companies have not provided a detailed deployment schedule or specified how many sites will become operational in the first phase.

title: Sunken WWII US cargo ship with 1,400 tons of explosives made safer
content: A sunken U.S. warship, SS Richard Montgomery, long regarded as a ticking time bomb because it still houses approximately 1,400 tonnes of unexploded ammunition onboard, has been made slightly safer eight decades after it sank.Engineers removed the ship’s three masts from the fragile wreck as experts feared they could collapse one day and potentially trigger an explosion.“The vessel was starting to lean and deteriorate, so they could see some of the structures around the mast starting to collapse,” said Nolan, an architect with marine salvage firm Resolve Marine Group that carried out the mast removal operation last month.Mast’s fall could trigger explosionThe mast had remained visible above the water near Sheerness, a coastal town about 50 miles (80 km) east of London on the Thames Estuary, since the ship sank in 1944.The fear is the masts could have fallen onto the cargo itself, causing it to detonate,” he added.Before the operation, his team completed extensive surveys to understand the wreck site using radar, magnetometers and sonar systems.Special tools were then used to carry out the delicate operation, and extra caution was exercised to avoid any vibrations while approaching the wreck that may set off the unexploded bombs still inside the wreck.Divers carefully cut through the masts with a diamond wire, taking turns as they worked on the fragile deck. Although the masts remained well preserved, officials said the surrounding steel structure had become “paper thin.”The exact munitions left onboard the ship, nicknamed Monty, are yet unknown. A defense agency report projected that more than 2000 cluster bombs, white phosphorus smoke artillery, and around 300 blockbuster bombs weighing nearly 2000 pounds (900 kg) were still on the ship.The wreck continues to pose a potential hazard to nearby communities, although experts have divided views over how severe the consequences of an explosion would be.A 2004 report suggested that the blast Some could cause a small tsunami, hurling debris nearly 1.8 miles (3 kilometers) into the air, “shatter almost every window in Sheerness” and devastate the town. However, David Alexander, an emergency planning expert at University College London, wrote in a 2019 paper that considerable uncertainty remains over the true level of risk posed by the wreck.Masts preserved at MuseumBecause of their historical significance, the detached masts have been transferred to the Dockyard Chatham, a maritime museum in Kent.UK maritime minister Keir Mather welcomed the operation and said that the masts had put “significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site.”Built in 1943 at Jacksonville, Florida, the World War II cargo ship was carrying about 7,000 tonnes of ammunition to Britain. It was due to anchor near Sheerness after passing through the Thames Estuary, but dragged its anchor and ran aground on a sandbank. Although the crew unloaded about half of the cargo, a crack in the hull ultimately caused the ship to sink, leaving thousands of tonnes of explosives on the seabed.Besides removing the mast, the British government has long kept the area around the U.S. cargo ship as a shipping exclusion zone. Since last year, the government has also issued a no-fly zone for the area, and these restrictions will remain in force, the government said in a statement.​

title: China's Tencent Hy4 challenges world's top models with 7.2% error rate
content: China’s Tencent has introduced a new open-source AI model that can operate computers, interpret complex images, and tackle demanding engineering tasks. Called Hy4, the model marks Tencent’s latest attempt to compete with leading open-source AI systems.Hy4 adds visual understanding to Tencent’s Hy model family for the first time. It can process detailed images, interpret complicated charts, and solve mathematical problems involving visual information. The model also introduces computer-use capabilities, allowing it to interact with command-line tools and graphical interfaces.Tencent plans to publish Hy4’s model weights and system cards in the coming days. The company says it has also incorporated safeguards targeting cybersecurity and biological risks.Computer control gets smarterHy4 can operate professional software, including Blender and computer-aided design (CAD) applications. Tencent trained the model to handle complex workflows that require planning and multiple execution steps. These capabilities could help automate tasks that traditionally demand considerable manual input.The model also supports 3D scene creation, web development, and document production. Tencent reported an average evaluation score of 83.18 on its WorkBuddy platform. Hy4 achieved a 96.15 percent pass rate across evaluated tasks.It also ranked first in nine of 12 tested scenarios within mainland China. WorkBuddy integrates Hy4 with Tencent’s workplace collaboration software, WeCom. The integration lets the model access information across chats, emails, documents, calendars, and meetings.Hy4 can track project developments, identify unfinished assignments, and flag approaching deadlines. Tencent also plans to introduce additional team collaboration features through WorkBuddy’s upcoming Projects feature.Financial and coding advancesFinancial research represents another major application for Hy4. Tencent trained the model using thousands of specialized workspaces and tens of thousands of professional tasks. These exercises covered fund research, securities analysis, and quantitative investment strategies.In a blind evaluation involving 213 financial professionals, Hy4 achieved the highest overall score. The assessment included 579 real-world financial tasks. Tencent said approximately 70 percent of participating professionals had over five years of industry experience.Hy4 scored 3.04, narrowly ahead of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 at 2.97. Kimi K3.1 Pro and GLM-5.3 both recorded 2.68.Software development also received attention during training. Hy4 improved its GameDev benchmark score by 19.1 percent over Hy4 Preview. Its GameLogic score increased by another 9.8 percent.The model supports development workflows involving Unreal Engine, Unity, and Godot. Tencent says these improvements extend to complex game mechanics and multiplayer implementations.Lower costs and safety measuresTencent has also worked to reduce factual errors when Hy4 retrieves information. Internal evaluations showed its hallucination rate falling from 12.95 percent to 7.2 percent. Errors linked to unsupported assumptions dropped from 23.1 percent to 5.6 percent.Cybersecurity safeguards form another part of the release. Tencent trained Hy4 on defensive security material, including vulnerability analysis and remediation. The training excludes offensive exploitation materials, according to the company.Hy4 is available through Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, CodeBuddy, Yuanbao, and several other platforms. Its API also supports third-party services, including OpenRouter and OpenCode.Pricing remains unchanged from Hy4 Preview despite the reported performance improvements. Tencent charges approximately $0.90 per million input tokens and $2.70 per million output tokens. A cached input million costs approximately $0.045.Tencent also plans to release Hy4 Flash soon. The smaller offering will target applications where lower operating costs matter most.

title: New zinc-ion batteries retain 90% capacity after 10,000 cycles
content: Current zinc-based batteries often have relatively short lifespans because their materials gradually degrade during repeated charge-discharge cycles.By changing the chemistry of the battery’s cathode, Chinese researchers have developed a new liquid zinc-ion battery that retains nearly 90 percent of its capacity even after more than 10,000 charge-discharge cycles.According to the team, this corresponds to more than 3,500 hours of continuous operation.The researchers said their strategy could help pave the way for designing longer-lasting aqueous energy storage systems.Altered chemistry improves lifespanExisting aqueous zinc-ion batteries (ZIBs) typically rely on iodine-based cathodes because they offer long cycling stability, fast charge-discharge capability, and the potential to store large amounts of energy.However, iodine-based cathodes also suffer from several limitations. They conduct electricity poorly, undergo structural changes as the battery charges and discharges, and allow iodine ions to migrate through the battery. This so-called shuttle effect reduces efficiency, accelerates material degradation, and shortens battery life.To overcome these challenges, researchers from Jilin University and the Changchun Institute of Applied Chemistry modified the functional group chemistry of the cathode to develop self-supporting carbon nanotube cathodes (SSCC).In their experiments, they compared the iodine adsorption capability of modified carbon nanotubes with that of unmodified ones. The team investigated nanotubes functionalized with hydroxyl (‒OH), carboxyl (‒COOH), and amine (‒NH₂) groups to determine which surface chemistry performed best.Using spectroscopy and microscopy techniques, the researchers confirmed the successful introduction of the functional groups and the uniform loading of iodine throughout the cathode material.They found that the hydroxyl-modified nanotubes acted like tiny anchors, trapping iodine ions where they belonged rather than letting them migrate through the battery. This reduced energy loss while improving both efficiency and long-term stability.Laboratory tests showed that the new cathode stored a high amount of electrical charge, delivering an initial reversible capacity of 175.5 mAh/g (milliampere-hours per gram) at a current density of 1 A/g (ampere per gram) while maintaining excellent durability.Even after more than 10,000 charge-discharge cycles, the battery retained 89.34 percent of its original capacity.At a higher current density of 10 A/g, the battery delivered a capacity of 120 mAh/g while achieving an exceptionally long cycling life of 93,400 charge-discharge cycles.Shuttle effect lostAdvanced characterization techniques, including in situ Raman spectroscopy performed during battery operation and ex situ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy conducted after cycling, confirmed that the iodine species were repeatedly and reversibly converted during charging and discharging.The researchers also found that the modified cathode effectively eliminated the unwanted iodine shuttle effect, preventing iodine ions from lingering in the electrolyte, reducing energy loss, and improving battery stability.To demonstrate practical potential, the team built a larger pouch-cell prototype containing 150 mg of iodine. The battery operated at 1.1 volts, delivered an actual capacity of 23.8 mAh, and retained 91.7 percent of its original capacity after 350 charge-discharge cycles, demonstrating promising performance under more realistic operating conditions.The researchers concluded that modifying the cathode’s functional group chemistry provides a simple and effective way to improve iodine conversion kinetics while stabilizing aqueous zinc-iodine batteries. They added that the approach could guide the future design of long-life aqueous energy storage systems based on naturally abundant zinc metal.The findings were published in Science China Chemistry.​

title: Drone that can travel faster than speed of sound to get power boost
content: A new type of supersonic target drone is set to get a major boost with the help of turbojet engines. Texas-based Safran Power Units will supply its turbojet engines for the supersonic target drone. Called the Falcon Supersonic UAV, the drone is being developed by UVAD Technologies Inc.UVAD claims that as a multi-role platform, Falcon can serve as an introductory counter-hypersonic system and can be adapted for high-speed ISR, function as an interceptor, or operate alongside fighter jets as an attritable high-speed UAV.Supersonic drone to be powered by two turbojet engines Falcon will be powered by two turbojet engines provided by Safran Power Units, delivering robustness, reliability, and extended lifespan, far exceeding current industry standards.Safran Power Units’ engines will enable the Falcon to reach supersonic speeds at low and medium altitudes, while ensuring rapid deployment and recovery. This level of performance allows for more frequent and cost-effective training sessions for air, naval, and missile defense operators, according to a press release.“We are particularly pleased to be entering into this partnership with Safran Power Units, a globally recognised expert in the field of high-performance and affordable turbojet engines,” said David Birkett, UVAD Technologies Inc. CEO.“Our two companies share a common vision for high-performance, affordable defence systems capable of addressing the challenges of the future, particularly those posed by supersonic threats.”This strategic collaboration combines UVAD’s innovation in aerospace and defense with Safran Power Units’ global excellence in propulsion technology. Beyond today’s training needs, this partnership anticipates tomorrow’s challenges by offering armed forces an adaptable solution. With its modular architecture and autonomous flight system, Falcon embodies the shared ambition of Safran Power Units and UVAD to make advanced defense technology more accessible and adaptable to evolving operational environments. This innovative system will notably allow a single operator to oversee multiple drones simultaneously, optimizing the efficiency and flexibility of training scenarios, as per the release.Propulsion system for supersonic drone“We are excited to start this partnership with UVAD to provide the propulsion system for their Falcon drone,” said Ghislaine Doukhan, Safran Power Units CEO. “The choice of our engines will make a significant contribution to the Falcon’s capabilities in terms of supersonic flight, robustness, and cost-effectiveness.”Falcon’s supersonic speed, aerodynamic design, and high maneuverability enable it to execute complex flight patterns and evasive maneuvers, making it a powerful asset for both training scenarios and real-world operational deployments, according to the company.The drone is equipped with advanced autonomous flight systems, and the platform enables operators to control multiple units simultaneously, enhancing mission efficiency and reducing manpower requirements.UVAD also highlighted that Falcon’s containerized design allows for easy transport and setup, while the pneumatic catapult launch system eliminates the need for a runway, allowing for maximized mission flexibility in dynamic environments. The drone offers a speed of 1.6 Mach and payload capacity of 110 lbs. Falcon is an innovative, affordable, and reusable supersonic aerial target designed to support the increasingly sophisticated missile defence training required by the armed forces.

title: A Hidden Star May Be Plowing Through Betelgeuse’s Giant Atmosphere
content:
This artist’s illustration shows the smaller, hotter companion star Siwarha creating a wake-like disruption in Betelgeuse’s outer atmosphere as it orbits directly through it. The shape of Betelgeuse itself becomes slightly oblong as a result of Siwarha’s perturbations. Credit: NSF/AUI/NSF NRAO/M. Weiss
Radio images suggest a link between Betelgeuse’s changing outline and its companion’s expected orbit, offering clues to how a smaller star may influence a giant’s later life.
Betelgeuse, the bright red supergiant marking Orion’s shoulder, may have another star stirring its atmosphere from within. Its recently identified companion, Siwarha, is thought to orbit at a distance of only about twice the giant’s radius. New radio observations suggest that this close neighbor is leaving a visible mark on the shape of Betelgeuse’s outer gas, even though the companion itself is too faint to appear in those observations.
Researchers proposed Siwarha’s existence in 2024 to explain Betelgeuse’s mysterious 2,100-day brightness cycle. Direct imaging and spectroscopic studies of the star’s light have since supported its existence. The companion’s name means “her bracelet,” a reference to Betelgeuse’s Arabic meaning, “the hand of al-Jawza.”
Betelgeuse’s shape hints at Siwarha’s influence
The new study was led by Dr. Lynn D. Matthews, Principal Research Scientist and Assistant Director at MIT Haystack Observatory, with colleagues from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, the University of Manchester, and the European Southern Observatory. The team combined observations from the U.S. National Science Foundation’s Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (NSF VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), collected between 2021 and 2026 at seven radio frequencies ranging from 22 to 485 GHz.
Radio waves at different frequencies reveal different depths in a star’s atmosphere. Using both observatories allowed the researchers to build a picture of Betelgeuse layer by layer, from just above its visible surface to several times the star’s radius.
“It was the combination of the incredible data from the NSF VLA and ALMA that gave us a convincing result here,” said Matthews. “The fact that we can use these facilities to actually resolve the disks of nearby stars is amazing.”
Detecting Siwarha directly was beyond the observations’ reach. The team calculated that the companion would be tens to hundreds of times too faint to see at radio wavelengths. They could, however, measure the ellipticity of Betelgeuse’s radio-emitting atmosphere, meaning how stretched or egg-shaped it appeared, at different observing times.
The atmosphere looked noticeably more elongated near the times when Siwarha was expected to be at its greatest apparent separation from Betelgeuse. It appeared rounder when the companion was expected to pass in front of or behind the giant star. That correspondence suggests that the smaller star’s gravity and movement are disturbing the surrounding gas.
“This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere,” Matthews explained. Its passage could leave a wake, much as a boat leaves one as it moves through water.
The team will need observations covering more of Siwarha’s orbit, particularly at frequencies that have not yet been well sampled, to confirm and refine these findings.
Warming again after the Great Dimming
The same radio data also show that Betelgeuse’s extended atmosphere has largely recovered from a much more conspicuous disturbance. In late 2019 and early 2020, the star faded to its faintest level in more than a century of record-keeping. During that episode, known as the Great Dimming, Betelgeuse ejected a billion tons of stellar material that partially blocked our view.
Months before the dimming, a 2019 study led by Matthews had found that Betelgeuse’s atmosphere was unusually cool at radio wavelengths. That team proposed that convection, the circulation of gas carrying heat from deep within the star, had triggered a shock wave. The wave could have disturbed gas in the outer layers, setting the stage for the massive dust-forming outburst that followed.
The new measurements show that the atmosphere’s brightness temperature, a temperature inferred from the strength of its radio emission, has returned to more typical levels at those same wavelengths. At a distance from the center of about 2.7 times Betelgeuse’s radius, the gas now registers around 3,500 kelvin, or about 5,840°F. That is comparable to the temperature of the star’s visible surface.
A temperature dip above Betelgeuse’s surface
Closer to the surface, the highest-frequency ALMA measurements revealed a much cooler layer. These observations probed nearer to Betelgeuse’s surface than previous radio measurements and found temperatures of roughly 2,200 kelvin, or about 3,500°F. That is more than 1,000 kelvin cooler than the photosphere, the star’s visible surface.
The measurements confirm a long-suspected “temperature minimum” between the photosphere and the chromosphere, an atmospheric layer above it. This cool region coincides with the “MOLsphere,” a shell of molecular gas that astronomers had long inferred from infrared observations but had rarely examined so directly at radio wavelengths.
Future observatories, including the Next Generation Very Large Array now in development, are expected to make such detailed studies more routine. Sharper views could help researchers understand how red supergiants shed material and evolve in the final stages of their lives, and how the gravitational pull of a nearby companion might shape that process.
Reference: “New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion” by L. D. Matthews, A. K. Dupree, A. M. S. Richards and W. R. F. Dent, 32 August 2026,

title: A Black Hole Could Split in Two, According to a Surprising New Theory
content:
A startling new theory suggests that black holes spinning at extreme speeds might split in two, challenging what scientists thought possible. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
Black holes might split in two under extreme conditions, theoretical calculations suggest, offering physicists a way to explore the limits of our understanding of gravity.
Two black holes can collide and merge into one. But could a single black hole divide into two smaller ones that go their separate ways? Reversing a merger might sound straightforward, but the rules governing black holes make it difficult.
The entropy barrier to splitting
One obstacle is entropy, a measure of how many different microscopic arrangements can give a physical system the same overall properties. Think of rolling two dice. Several combinations produce a total of seven, but only two ones produce a total of two. Entropy captures a similar distinction between an overall result and the different underlying arrangements that can produce it. More possible arrangements mean higher entropy.
For an ordinary black hole that is not rotating, two smaller black holes would have less combined entropy than the original. That makes splitting thermodynamically unfavorable. The usual requirement of thermodynamics is that the total entropy of an isolated system should stay the same or increase, rather than decrease.
Whether black holes can split is the subject of “When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies,” a theoretical study published in
Physical Review D
. The unusual title describes what a split would look like through time. A black hole’s outer boundary, called its horizon, would trace a trouser-like shape, with one section dividing into two “legs.”
Illustration of black hole splitting in two creating the shape of pants. Credit: Francesco Sannino
“In our study, we investigate which physical laws normally prevent a black hole from splitting into two. We also investigate if certain circumstances may allow a split to happen”, says Francesco Sannino, a co-author and professor of physics at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy and the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark.
Sannino’s co-authors are Giacomo Cacciapaglia, a Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS) researcher at the Laboratoire de Physique Théorique et Hautes Énergies, a joint laboratory of CNRS and Sorbonne Université in Paris, and Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark.
Rapid rotation offers a possible loophole
Their calculations suggest that rapid rotation could offer a loophole in the thermodynamic barrier. A spinning black hole might be able to divide under conditions that would make splitting unfavorable for a nonrotating one.
“But the two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate,” says Francesco Sannino.
Uncertain odds beyond Einstein’s theory
The researchers also explore theories with additional dimensions of space. Within these theories, physicists already know of black-hole-like objects that can become unstable and begin to break apart. Under some of these conditions, splitting can be thermodynamically favorable, particularly when one resulting black hole is much smaller than the other. Even then, showing that entropy permits a split does not establish that the process will actually happen.
The possibilities also extend to primordial black holes, hypothetical objects that could have formed in the early universe.
“We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einstein’s theory, and we are working to quantify this. We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers,” says Francesco Sannino.
Reference: “When black holes admit pair-of-pants topologies” by Giacomo Cacciapaglia, Manuel Del Piano, Francesco Sannino and Vania Vellucci, 22 October 2026,

title: Study Reveals How Brain Function Changes When We Learn Something New
content:
Scientists have detected measurable changes in brain activity after beginners completed just one violin lesson. Credit: Shutterstock
A beginner’s violin lesson may seem worlds apart from dementia research, yet wearable brain scans are revealing signals that could help scientists understand both learning and neurological disease.
Playing a familiar tune on a violin is no simple task for someone who has never held the instrument. Each movement must produce the intended sound, and the brain has to learn how to coordinate those movements. Researchers at the University of Nottingham have now captured changes in brain activity as beginners learned to play, revealing measurable differences after just one violin lesson.
The study, published in the journal
Imaging Neuroscience
, involved 22 novice violin players. Using a wearable brain scanner, the scientists tracked patterns of neural activity while participants attempted to play “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.” They found that those who improved the most also showed the greatest changes in certain brain signals associated with movement and learning.
A metal-free violin enables brain scans
Capturing those signals while someone plays an instrument presents a technical challenge. The electrical activity of neurons generates extremely weak magnetic fields, which can be measured to study brain function. However, the equipment must be sensitive enough to detect these signals without interference, while still allowing the person being studied to move naturally.
The researchers used a technology called OPM-MEG, developed in Nottingham, that incorporates brain-scanning sensors into a lightweight helmet connected to a backpack-mounted control unit. Unlike scanning systems that restrict movement, this wearable design allows researchers to monitor brain activity as people perform everyday tasks.
There was still one problem. A conventional violin contains metal components that would interfere with the scanner’s measurements.
To overcome this obstacle, the team enlisted Alan Kirby, an expert violinist and violin maker from Nottingham. Kirby sourced a standard violin and replaced every metal part with alternatives he crafted himself, producing an entirely wooden instrument operating at frequencies associated with Baroque music.
“Bringing together the ancient art of violin making, with the quantum physics underpinning this brain scanner, has been amazing. Perhaps even more impressive was to actually see the effects of my lessons on peoples brains. That was quite an experience,” Kirby said.
Alan Kirby working on a Violin. Credit: University of Nottingham
Reading the brain’s musical predictions
Kirby also served as the participants’ violin instructor. At the beginning of the experiment, all 22 beginners watched a video of him playing “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.” They then attempted to perform the same melody during their first scanning session, while the researchers recorded their brain activity.
After completing that initial recording, the participants received a violin lesson from Kirby. They then returned for a second scanning session, following the same procedure and attempting to play the tune again. By comparing recordings from before and after the lesson, the researchers could examine how the brain responded to a brief period of musical training.
Their attention focused on brain waves, rhythmic fluctuations in electrical activity that occur across groups of neurons. In particular, they examined oscillations in the beta frequency range, which are thought to help signal whether an action produces the result the brain expects.
When learning the violin, that process could involve predicting the sound of a note before playing it and registering whether the actual sound matches the prediction. Unexpected notes provide information that the movement did not produce the intended outcome.
“Your brain works by making predictions about what will happen as a result of your actions. So, if I am playing a violin, my brain will have an expectation of what sound it will make. If I play the expected note, my brain receives information that the outcome matched its prediction; if I hit an unexpected note, it receives information that it did not. In this experiment, we were able to measure these signals in real time while the instrument was being played,” said Joe Gibson, a Ph.D. researcher in the School of Physics and Astronomy.
A participant plays the violin while wearing a specialized brain-scanning helmet that allows researchers to monitor neural activity in real time, revealing how the brain adapts as new motor skills are learned. Credit: University of Nottingham
Greater brain changes accompany better playing
The recordings revealed changes in beta-wave activity following the lesson, providing evidence that even a short period of musical instruction can alter measurable patterns of brain function. The researchers also found a relationship between those neural changes and improvements in playing ability.
Participants with the largest differences in beta-wave activity between the two scanning sessions also showed the greatest improvement in their violin performance. Although the findings do not establish that the changes in brain activity caused better playing, they suggest that beta oscillations are closely associated with how people acquire new motor skills.
Brain scanning could reach beyond music
Making these measurements possible required expertise extending well beyond neuroscience. Professor Matthew Brookes of the University of Nottingham’s School of Physics and Astronomy has spent more than a decade leading the development of OPM-MEG technology. The violin experiment brought together specialists in physics, engineering, mathematics, and music to create a system capable of studying movement as it happens.
“This is a study that we have been working on for years, and it’s taken a unique combination of skills: the physics required to measure brain activity; design engineering to create an ergonomic scanner that people can wear; the mathematics required to model the signals; and of course, Alan’s knowledge and abilities as a violin player and maker. Without this wonderful diversity of talent, we simply couldn’t have done the work.”
The researchers believe the technology could eventually help scientists investigate more than musical learning. Some of the patterns of brain activity measured during the experiment can also be affected by neurological conditions, including dementia. Studying these signals during natural movements could offer another way to examine how brain function changes in health and disease.
“The results provide a greater understanding of motor learning. It’s also fascinating that some of the effects that we measure here are among those that can be affected by disorders like dementia. Hopefully this type of study will bring about a new understanding of not just healthy brain function, but also disease,” said Brookes.
Reference: “Beta-band dynamics during a naturalistic motor task: an OPM-MEG study” by Joseph Gibson, Jessikah Fildes, Alan Kirby, Niall Holmes, Lukas Rier, Karen J. Mullinger, Matias Ison, Peter G. Morris, Elena Boto, Ryan M. Hill and Matthew J. Brookes, 27 July 2026,
DOI: 10.64898/2026.07.27.740561
Disclosure: The University launched a spin-out company, Cerca Magnetics Limited, in 2020 to commercialize OPM-MEG scanners and related technologies. The wearable system has been installed in a number of high profile research institutions across the globe and is being used to investigate a range of neurological and psychiatric conditions, including epilepsy and dementia.

title: A Hidden Cancer-Fighting Switch Could Supercharge the Human Immune System
content:
A protein best known for preventing cancer may also help immune cells fight it. Researchers discovered that briefly activating this protein enhanced the ability of engineered human T cells to attack melanoma in laboratory experiments. Credit: Shutterstock
Temporarily activating a protein best known for preventing cancer helped engineered human immune cells kill melanoma cells more effectively in the lab, suggesting a way to improve existing cell therapies.
Engineering a patient’s immune cells to recognize cancer does not guarantee that they will keep fighting it. Repeated exposure to cancer can gradually weaken T cells’ ability to multiply and attack tumors, a decline known as exhaustion. The laboratory process used to prepare these cells for treatment can also make them mature too quickly, reducing their chances of surviving and remaining effective over time.
These problems limit engineered T-cell therapies, including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy and T-cell receptor (TCR) therapy. Both involve collecting a patient’s immune cells, genetically modifying them in a laboratory to recognize cancer, and infusing them back into the patient to attack tumors. Such treatments have transformed care for certain blood cancers and are increasingly being investigated for solid tumors.
Researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have identified a possible way to improve these cells during preparation. Their study, published in
Frontiers in Immunology
, found that temporarily activating a protein called p53 helped human T cells develop characteristics associated with longer-lasting immune responses and become more effective at killing melanoma cells in the laboratory.
Activating p53 improves melanoma cell killing
Often called the “guardian of the genome,” p53 is best known for preventing damaged cells from becoming cancerous. Scientists have extensively studied that protective role, but its involvement in regulating human T cells is less understood.
The team collected human T cells and treated them with navtemadlin, an investigational drug that increases p53 activity by blocking another protein, MDM2. Normally, MDM2 keeps p53 levels under control. Comparing treated and untreated cells allowed the researchers to assess how activating p53 affected their development, energy production, and ability to fight cancer.
T cells (black) attack melanoma cells (red). Compared with the control group (left), T cells treated with navtemadlin were significantly more effective at killing melanoma cells, leaving very few cancer cells remaining. Credit: Crompton Laboratory
To test cancer-killing performance, the researchers genetically engineered T cells to recognize a protein found on certain melanoma cells. They then used specialized imaging equipment to monitor the cells for nearly seven days.
The engineered T cells prepared with navtemadlin were significantly more effective at killing melanoma cells than untreated cells. Their advantage became apparent after approximately 40 hours and continued throughout the experiment. They also showed improved cancer-fighting activity without additional interleukin-2, a protein commonly used to support T-cell growth and survival.
“This is one of the first studies to link p53, one of the most extensively studied proteins in biology, to T-cell exhaustion in humans,” said Joseph Crompton, MD, PhD, assistant professor of surgery at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA and senior author of the study. “While p53 has long been known for its role in preventing cancer, our findings suggest it may also play an important role in helping immune cells maintain their ability to fight it. This opens up a new avenue for developing more effective cancer immunotherapies.”
More energy, fewer signs of exhaustion
The treated cells had greater energy reserves and were more likely to produce interferon-gamma and granzyme B, two cancer-fighting proteins that help immune cells coordinate an attack and destroy cancer cells.
They were also more likely to develop into central memory T cells, which have a greater capacity to survive and multiply when they encounter their target again. Along with fewer molecular signs of exhaustion, this shift suggested that the cells might remain effective for longer. Those characteristics indicate potential for lasting immune responses, although the experiments tested human cells in the laboratory rather than treatment outcomes in patients.
Cell survival depends on the dose
Adding a drug such as navtemadlin during cell preparation could potentially fit into existing manufacturing processes. That would offer a way to improve engineered T-cell therapies without developing an entirely new treatment or introducing additional genetic modifications.
At lower concentrations, navtemadlin encouraged the development of healthy memory T cells without substantially reducing the overall number of viable cells. Higher concentrations, however, caused more cells to die, showing why any use of this approach would require careful control of p53 activation.
Reference: “p53 activation via pharmacologic MDM2 inhibition constrains exhaustion and enhances antitumor function of human CD8+ T cells” by Alexandra Boix de Jesus, Hy B. Dao, Anthony Imani, Gabriel A. Rodriguez, Michael S. Shehata, Rachana R. Chandran, Stuart A. Fine, Sin Y. Lim, Michelle To, Serena Y. Lofftus, Nicolas Pedroncelli, Fritz C. Eilber, Brigitte N. Gomperts, Tyler R. McCaw, Cristina Puig-Saus and Joseph G. Crompton, 18 September 2026,
Frontiers in Immunology
DOI: 10.3389/fimmu.2026.1910235
