title: California Sends AI Safety Lawmaker to Congress
content: Scott Wiener , the California politician who led the successful effort to pass AI safety legislation in the state’s legislature last year, is headed to Washington. The state senator won Tuesday’s election to succeed long-time House Speaker Nancy Pelosi , after his opponent conceded on Wednesday. When Wiener arrives in D.C., he will be among the few members of Congress to have authored significant AI legislation. Last year, Calif. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Wiener’s SB 53 , which requires the largest AI companies to write and comply with their own safety policies for managing severe risks from their technology. The bill and the AI companies that supported it could indicate the kind of AI policies that a Democrat-controlled Congress will get behind. “Scott was working on these frontier AI safety issues before it was cool,” Nathan Calvin , chief strategy officer at Encode AI , an AI policy organization that backed SB 53, told me Wednesday. Calvin said he hopes the next Congress will go further than the state bill, including by requiring AI companies to work with embedded independent evaluators and test the safety of their models. Indeed, Wiener campaigned on a promise to build on SB 53 at the national level, including by creating a federal regulatory body for AI and expanding unemployment insurance to guard against AI job displacement—a concern Anthropic leaders frequently raise. SB 53 also provides whistleblower protections and requires AI companies to report to state officials if their models are involved in safety incidents, such as theft of a model that is then used to cause harm. While Congressional lawmakers have proposed a slew of bills to regulate frontier AI models, none have actually reached a floor vote. The most significant AI-related bill to be signed into law was the bipartisan Take It Down Act , which criminalized the publication of non-consensual sexual deepfake images. But supervision of leading models from labs like OpenAI and Anthropic has been left to the Trump administration, including a June executive order that created a voluntary framework for evaluating frontier models before they’re released to the public. Wiener has spent the last few years scrapping with the same big tech and venture capital firms that will try to shape future national legislation, an experience that should give the freshman Congressman a sense of where he’ll face headwinds. In 2024, Wiener’s SB 1047 , the predecessor bill to SB 53, drew significant opposition from Andreessen Horowitz , OpenAI, Google , Hugging Face , Meta and Y Combinator , which warned it would harm innovation. Anthropic opposed some elements, such as arguing its whistleblower protections were overly broad. Newsom ultimately vetoed that bill, but set up a working group whose recommendations informed SB 53. SB 53 ultimately won an endorsement from Anthropic, as well as some safety-minded investors. In fact, Anthropic went on to donate $40 million to Public First Action , an AI safety political organization that spent $3.5 million on a super PAC supporting Wiener’s campaign. However, none of Anthropic’s donation went toward Wiener’s election, according to a spokesperson for Public First Action. Anthropic’s donation is restricted to educational initiatives and cannot be used for political spending. (Though some employees of AI companies donated directly to the campaign, leading some of Wiener’s opponents to criticize him for receiving AI funding.) OpenAI initially lobbied against SB 53 . But in September, chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane wrote that OpenAI supported SB 53 , and last month the company wrote to Newsom recommending that California strengthen the regulation. Anthropic and OpenAI’s support for regulations has raised suspicions among tech notables such as David Sacks that the AI giants are attempting to pass policies that will favor their businesses by making compliance difficult for smaller startups. SB 53 tries to sidestep this concern by focusing on AI companies generating at least $500 million in annual revenue. In Congress’s absence, other states beside California have filled the policy vacuum: copycat bills in New York and Illinois followed California’s SB 53 this year, and Massachusetts is considering a bill of its own . These state laws have built on SB 53 by requiring independent compliance audits of AI companies. That’s an idea that is already catching on at the federal level, appearing in President Trump’s recent voluntary accord with AI companies, but has yet to be turned into national law. OpenAI, Andreessen Horowitz and other AI players have argued that a “patchwork” of state-level bills could become burdensome to AI companies, but several efforts by the federal government to preempt these state bills have flopped in the absence of a national replacement. If AI advocates do accept a preemption deal in the next Congress, Wiener’s platform offers some clues as to what a federal replacement for state laws could involve. “Exactly what is and isn't worth it on preemption is a hard question, but I do think Scott is one of the legislators that I would trust to really try to make that deal in the interest of the public,” said Nick Beckstead , co-founder and CEO of the Secure AI Project , another AI policy organization that sponsored SB 53. To be sure, Wiener will face an uphill battle as a junior member, especially as other Democrats clamor to advance their own bills. More broadly, any legislation faces steep odds in Congress thanks to Trump’s veto power. Still, Wiener will find some natural allies on the Hill. For example, Manny Rutinel , a Democrat who authored Colorado’s 2024 law against AI discrimination, won a seat in the House of Representatives during Tuesday’s election. However, Alex Bores , the state Assemblymember behind New York’s version of SB 53, the 2025 Raise Act , lost his Congressional primary over the summer. Here’s what else is going on… People on the Move Sequoia Capital , the venture capital firm that was an early investor in Google and YouTube and wrote the first check to Nvidia , is shutting down its London office, the company said on Wednesday. The firm is making a number of other structural changes and refocusing on Silicon Valley. Cat Wu , a product lead of Anthropic’s popular Claude Code product, announced that she would be joining OpenAI to lead product management for its core products. Overheard Microsoft said last week that it spent about $5 billion less on capital expenditures in the third quarter than it had previously projected because data center capacity it was planning to rent wasn’t ready on time. Microsoft didn’t name the “third party” behind those delays, but one of them is Iren , a publicly traded cloud provider that is already facing pressure as borrowing costs have risen, The Information reported . China has blocked SoftBank Group’s $5.4 billion acquisition of the robotics unit of ABB , a Swiss-Swedish electrical and automation technology company. The Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review , part of China’s powerful National Development and Reform Commission , told SoftBank that the deal will be prohibited, ABB said in a statement on Thursday. The same office earlier this year ordered the unwinding of Meta Platforms’ $2 billion acquisition of Chinese AI startup Manus . Earnings Report Uber plans to more than double the number of self-driving cars operating on its platform over the next year, the company said on Wednesday as it reported third quarter results, with plans to arrange financing to build self driving fleets of cars. Stocks of neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius dropped 9.9% and 6.7% respectively on Wednesday, even as most tech stocks rose, a sign that investors interpreted Tuesday’s votes in favor of anti-data center candidates as particularly bad for newer cloud firms. Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Isomorphic Labs , which uses AI to discover new medicines, is in talks to raise about $5 billion at a roughly $50 billion valuation. AMD agreed to acquire Taalas , which designs specialized AI inference chips, in a cash-and-stock transaction valued at about $2.9 billion , including up to $1.4 billion in contingent consideration. Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , which tracks passwords and authentication credentials used by AI agents, for a reported $500 million . Nooks , which uses AI agents to automate sales calls and prospecting, secured a $500 million growth-capital commitment from General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund. Laza Medical , which makes AI-powered robotic imaging for heart procedures, raised up to $160 million in a Series B funding round led by GE HealthCare. Sentra , which helps companies keep AI agents from misusing sensitive data, raised $150 million in a Series C funding round led by Capital One Ventures. Pliant , which lets AI agents make business payments, raised $80 million in a Series C funding round led by Seaya Nova and Speedinvest. Rivio , which uses AI to manage hospital billing, raised $33 million (R$180 million) at a $200 million valuation in an extension of its Series A funding round led by Valor Capital Group. Supa , which uses AI to run UK apartment-block management firms, raised £21 million (about $28 million ) in a seed funding round led by 2150 and OpenOcean. Brava Security , which uses AI agents to simulate attacks and test security defenses, raised $15 million in a seed funding round led by Pitango and F2 Venture Capital. Finpilot , which uses AI agents to help institutional investors with research and reporting, raised $10 million in a Series A funding round led by Lobby Capital. Atmospheric AI , which uses AI to track raw-material supply chains, raised $10 million in a seed funding round led by DBL Partners. Meta has acquired AI coding startup Conductor . Apple lowered its AI budget for some engineers from $300 to $200 in an attempt to rein in its AI spending, with further cuts to as little as $100 for some teams, Bloomberg reported Wednesday. title: How a Claims Investor Got Kalshi to Open a Market on the NCAA Payout
content: Kalshi wants to become a major challenger to traditional financial markets by encouraging big funds and companies to use prediction markets to protect against losses. Behind the scenes, it’s developing new contracts to win those big investors over. That includes wagers aimed at niche corners of finance like the market for legal claims, where investors buy up claims at a discount betting they’ll be worth more once settlements are resolved. Last month, at a big investor’s request, Kalshi added new prediction contracts on the timing and size of payouts in the $2.8 billion settlement between college athletes and the National Collegiate Athletic Association. The idea came from investment firm Grand Teton Systems, which has bought about $400 million worth of claims from athletes. Louis d’Origny, co-founder of GTS, said he reached out to Kalshi because he wanted a way for claim holders to hedge the risk that the payments might come in smaller or later than expected. Under a court-approved settlement from last year, the NCAA is due to distribute back pay to college athletes who said they were illegally barred from sharing in revenue it made from broadcasting their games or using their name, image and likeness. But female athletes have challenged the settlement, saying they aren’t getting their fair share compared to male athletes, and that has put payouts on hold. The size and timing of individual payouts remains a question, which could also mean different tax implications for claimants based on when the back pay hits. Though Kalshi offers yes-no bets on everything from election outcomes and sports to “Dancing With the Stars” weekly winners—and even the outcome of some high-profile court decisions like Trump’s BBC lawsuit and Amazon’s antitrust case—it didn’t have any contracts to make wagers on how the NCAA settlement will play out. D’Origny said he suggested new contracts tied to some of the yet-to-be-resolved details. About 72 hours later, two new contracts went live on Kalshi— one allowing customers to bet on whether women will get a bigger share of the back pay and a second on when payments will begin. “Whats exciting is that this is a genuine hedging opportunity for real world risk,” d’Origny said. Kalshi and rival Polymarket both see a major growth opportunity in courting big traders to their platforms, arguing that they can use its contracts much as they would traditional futures contracts to hedge against things like interest rate changes or fluctuations in prices of commodities such as oil. Kalshi, which announced last week it had raised $1 billion at a $40 billion valuation, says that as of September it worked with 500 institutional customers making up around 25% of its trading volume. Both businesses are still dominated by sports betting, which accounts for about 90% of trading volume on each platform, and having more financial customers could also help with the prediction markets’ regulatory standing. Sports predictions in particular have drawn the ire of lawmakers and embroiled Kalshi, Polymarket and other competitors in lawsuits from dozens of states over accusations that the firms are running illegal gambling operations. Prediction markets offer more types of bets than traditional futures markets, creating the opportunity for entirely new forms of hedges. But high-profile examples of businesses using prediction market contracts have so far mostly involved hedgers using existing contracts. They’ve included a bar in New York hedging a free drinks promotion during the National Basketball Association finals and a Los Angeles ice cream shop betting on colder weather to insure against lower sales. And while Kalshi has announced it’s worked with investors like Ark Invest to develop new contracts, the examples it has cited include bets on topics with broad interest, like non-farm payroll numbers. That makes GTS’ request an interesting test case for Kalshi’s efforts to grow its institutional business. Large class-action settlements or major bankruptcies often attract investment firms because they involve thousands of claimants who may be enticed by an up-front payment payment, especially in complex cases that could take years to shake out. Notably, GTS became the largest buyer of claims in the bankruptcy of Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX. D’Origny, himself an FTX creditor, spotted an opportunity to buy bankruptcy claims at a discount from others who wanted a quick payout. GTS launched a website called FTXCreditor to solicit claims and eventually took ownership of almost 5,000 FTX claims. The long-running dispute between college athletes and the NCAA, which covers athletes who competed as far back as 2016, is proving to be another opportunity for GTS. The firm has been running a website encouraging athletes to sell their settlement claims to receive immediate cash. The website notes that almost 6,000 athletes have opted in so far. The contracts Kalshi created for d’Origny so far have drawn meager volume, and GTS itself hasn’t traded them yet because it hasn’t seen a favorable position to take. “We would hedge more exposure if we saw interesting odds,” d’Origny said. But d’Origny said the markets offer other benefits, because athletes who sell a claim to GTS could use the markets to place bets that could boost their total payoff. “This actually competes with our product offering,” he said. “We take on the risk entirely for athletes. Here they have a new avenue.” The contracts could also offer free marketing for GTS’ efforts to buy up claims. “People talking about the settlement might encourage some to sell,” he said.

title: Palo Alto Networks in Talks to Pay $500 Million for AI Security Startup
content: Palo Alto Networks is in talks to buy three-year-old Israeli security startup Clutch Security for around $500 million, according to people familiar with the matter. If finalized, the acquisition would be the fifth Palo Alto Networks has announced this year, as CEO Nikesh Arora seeks to bolster the company’s products that counter new AI threats. Clutch develops software that helps companies track passwords and authentication codes used by AI agents. Discussions are ongoing and may not lead to a deal. A Palo Alto Networks spokesperson said the company doesn’t comment about “rumors or speculation.” A spokesperson for Clutch Security didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The startup has raised more than $20 million from investors including Lightspeed Venture Partners and SignalFire. Its current valuation couldn’t be learned. The acquisition could further deepen Palo Alto Networks’ offerings in identity security—the software that helps businesses manage logins and other permissions to make sure their users only access the data they’re supposed to. Earlier this year, Palo Alto, which has a market cap of $287 billion, completed its $25 billion acquisition for CyberArk, the market leader in identity security. While CyberArk had historically focused on managing human users’ logins, Clutch tries to corral AI agents’ use of passwords and data. The cybersecurity sector has found its services in high demand from rising AI-related threats, as new AI models have shown they can find serious flaws in widely used software that attackers can exploit. Meanwhile, a string of high-profile incidents involving AI agents that have breached other companies’ systems has highlighted the need for security that labels, tracks and controls customers’ AI agents. These risks have spurred a string of acquisitions for startups that provide safeguards against AI agent blunders. Last month, HR and finance company Workday acquired startup C1.ai to manage AI agent identities alongside human identities. In August, identity security company Okta acquired Permiso Security and rival Sailpoint acquired Entro Security in June, both due to the targets’ specialization in managing AI agent identities.

title: Voters’ Gift to Big Tech
content: Voters just handed big tech a gift—and we’re not just thinking of Californians who voted against the billionaire tax proposal. (Can all those billionaires come home now?) Wednesday’s rally in the stocks of Amazon, Microsoft, Apple and Alphabet suggests that investors see lots of upside for those tech firms from Tuesday’s Democratic victory. The vote put a lot of people into office who are no fans of AI and data centers. By implication, any slowdown in AI data center development will disproportionately hurt neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius—which haven’t built out their facilities as much as bigger and older cloud firms. Notably, both their stocks dropped sharply Wednesday. On the theory that anything that hurts your rivals is good for you, that’s good for big cloud firms Amazon, Microsoft and Google. A forced AI slowdown might even allow big tech firms to pull back on capital expenditures, which investors would love. (For our in-depth look at the implications of Tuesday’s vote, see here and here . Today’s edition of TITV is also worth catching for smart interviews on the election’s ramifications with investor and political strategist Bradley Tusk, nonprofit official Charles Hua and Wall Street analyst CJ Muse.) Not all of tech stock’s reaction was related to AI, of course: The Democratic takeover might also lead to an end to the Iran war and maybe curtail President Donald Trump’s tariff addiction, both of which would be good for big tech firms. There’s also just the reality that markets hate uncertainty and the election result has given us a little bit more certainty, even if it has created a new set of questions. Still, given the potential upside of the election outcome for big tech companies, it’s a bit ironic how much tech folks have bad-mouthed the Democrats over the past few years. Then again, plenty of techies are facing tougher times ahead. Aside from the stocks of the neoclouds, stocks of chip designers like Nvidia and memory chip companies Micron and SK Hynix also sold off, reflecting the fact that they all rely on continued AI data center expansion for their revenue growth. Elon Musk, who spent a fortune trying to stop the Democrats, can’t expect too much love from them now. But as our story noted, it’s unclear how much he’ll really suffer. To be sure, this is all premature (but preparing analysis without all the facts in hand is what reporters do!). It’s going to take quite a while for us to figure out how the new state moratoriums on data center development will actually play out. Some people think that those who oppose data centers will soften their tone when they realize the impact on jobs in their community. “I would hope that cooler heads would…come to realize how important AI compute is,” said Cantor’s CJ Muse on TITV Wednesday. The best part of Wednesday’s reaction might have been the jokes on X. The award has to go to this one —that Republicans are “in talks to be acquired by Bending Spoons.” Perfect. Snap’s Community Quick question: Is someone who visits your app once a month as valuable as someone who visits every day? That’s not difficult to answer, right? Any company reliant on advertising (like Snap) theoretically wants more-frequent users. Snap doesn’t see it that way, however. The company reported on Wednesday that it plans to make monthly active users its “primary audience metric,” a shift away from the “daily active user” it has long relied on. Snap says that’s because MAU “represents the scale of our community.” In other words, more people use Snap once a month than once a day. Indeed, Snap says it has 977 million worldwide monthly users, nearly twice as many as its 495 million daily active users. And its daily user counts in the U.S. and Europe have declined over the past year—although they’ve grown everywhere else—which is something that looks bad for the company. Still, you have to wonder what’s next. Will Snap shift to yearly active users if the monthly user count starts to weaken? In Other News • Uber plans to more than double the number of self-driving cars operating on its platform over the next year, the company said on Wednesday as it reported third-quarter results, with plans to arrange financing to build self-driving fleets of cars. Uber also wants to bring in outside capital to help with that effort, Chief Financial Officer Balaji Krishnamurthy said. • OpenAI on Wednesday said it was buying Pierre Computer Co., a three-year-old startup that builds software tools to help developers manage and review code. • Charge Robotics’ chief technology officer, Max Justicz, said he used a specialized OpenAI model to find a vulnerability in a popular open-source software app that would allow someone to hack into major data centers. • The Department of Justice last week subpoenaed payroll startup Rippling, seeking all documents produced during discovery in an alleged corporate espionage lawsuit the company is waging against rival startup Deel, according to court filings. • Stablecoin issuer Circle reported that third-quarter revenue jumped 17% to $875 million, reflecting mostly a one-time bump from a token sale. title: Six Ways the Blue Wave Could Shake Up AI, Crypto and Tech
content: Democrats’ stunning victories in Tuesday’s election can at least partly be attributed to the fact that they capitalized on growing voter anxiety about AI and tech. What exactly lawmakers do with their newfound political power to address those anxieties remains to be seen, though. One of their biggest priorities is likely to be more regulation of data centers, since voters overwhelmingly backed state and federal candidates who supported moratoriums on their construction. But data center pauses were not the only AI issue on the ballot: AI safety also became a central talking point for prominent candidates like Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who was elected to the Senate on Tuesday night. “When we started all of these projects politically a year ago now or so, the idea that AI would be as salient and seemingly driving a lot of the debate about what happened in the election was unanticipated,” said Brad Carson, a former Democratic congressman from Oklahoma who heads the Public First super PAC network, a political advocacy group focused on AI safety that received backing from Anthropic. “The moment has arrived.” Still, how long will the anti–data center sentiment last? How will more moratoriums on their construction impact providers of AI compute? And how will Democrats regulate crypto, and will they make life harder for Republican megadonor Elon Musk? Here are six possible outcomes for the tech industry from Tuesday’s election: A narrow window for legislative action. Growing fears about AI capabilities over the past few months have spurred a wave of legislative proposals across Congress, including comprehensive bipartisan packages that would establish frameworks for regulating frontier models from labs like OpenAI and Anthropic. Still, if Democrats had eked out a 51-seat majority in the Senate and a small edge in the House, they would have struggled to reach a filibuster-proof 60 votes in the Senate—and then faced the prospect of a veto from President Donald Trump. Instead, Democrats could end up with 55 seats in the Senate and more than 250 seats in the House of Representatives, representing a commanding majority for Trump’s last two years in office. The margin of that victory creates more optimism for passing legislation, Carson said. He predicted a sweeping bill on frontier AI regulation, similar to one floated by Reps. Sara Jacobs and Don Beyer earlier this year, would pass by the spring. Jay Carney, the former Obama White House press secretary and a longtime tech executive, said the Democrats’ majority raises the possibility of bipartisan legislation that is veto-proof—a two-thirds majority in the House and Senate—given the appetite among some Republican lawmakers to take action on AI regulation. He was hopeful that meant Democrats could be more ambitious than just holding corruption-focused oversight hearings and strive to pass bills. “People don’t want just trials in D.C.,” Carney said. “They want action.” Some AI proposals have focused on creating so-called independent verification organizations that audit frontier models and guardrails to prevent catastrophic risks, but Carson said the Democrats’ majority could spur lawmakers to push for even further action, such as creating new regulatory agencies to oversee the AI sector. Still, data center regulation, a key area of alarm among voters, will likely be left to the states. That being said, oversight will be a hallmark of Congress come January, with Democrats holding the gavel and dragging executives to Washington to testify. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” wrote Ed Markey, a Democratic senator from Massachusetts, on X on Tuesday night. Data center blowback isn’t going anywhere . While kitchen-table issues like rising food and gas prices drove voters to the polls, data centers still represented a top issue. In an exit poll conducted by NBC in 45 states, 23% of voters said data centers were “crucial” in thinking about their vote for Congress, with another 64% describing them as a major or minor factor. More tellingly, 43 out of 44 local ballot initiatives to restrict data centers won on Tuesday, with many over 70%. Carson said the issue is likely to dominate the 2028 election cycle given data centers’ unpopularity with voters. “This shows you where people’s heads are, and where people who are running for president in either party are going to have to go,” he said. “You don’t run into a freight train of an 80/20 issue that’s salient to people.” Adam Kovacevich, a former Google executive who leads the center-left trade group Chamber of Progress, cautioned that AI safety organizations are trying to elevate their causes by “piggybacking” on data centers. “The two issues are completely different,” he said. AI safety, he said, is trying to “persuade voters to take action against an existential risk, whereas data centers are about impacting your community in a way that people can see and feel.” Even if pervasive opposition to data centers doesn’t mean voters are also allergic to AI, however, the likelihood of new moratoriums across the country will still affect many companies reliant on the buildout. A gift to big tech margins. The election results sparked wildly different reactions among investors in tech stocks. Chip stocks dropped, as did shares of the most prominent neocloud, CoreWeave, which fell more than 9%. At the same time, the three largest cloud providers—Amazon, Microsoft and Google—saw their shares jump more than 7%, 6% and 4%, respectively, outpacing the 2% rise in the Nasdaq Composite Index. The contrasting reactions make perfect sense, though. If you’re an Nvidia or a memory chip supplier like SK Hynix, anything that interrupts the data center buildout is bad news. The same is true for CoreWeave, which is already facing tough questions about whether it can access capital to build future data centers and has no other business to fall back on. In a statement, a CoreWeave spokesperson said the company doesn’t anticipate that any “shifts in the political landscape” will impact its existing customer commitments. “While future policy changes could affect data center development broadly, CoreWeave has strong visibility into its pipeline and retains flexibility to adjust where and when we build,” the statement said. “These factors limit our exposure and give us confidence in our ability to serve customers.” By comparison, the hyperscalers all have diversified portfolios of products. New data center pauses could stop future development plans, but most likely won’t impact the gigawatts’ worth of projects that are already underway. Even before the election, those companies’ investors were getting fidgety about the future capital expenditures these companies were planning. If data center legislation forces them to slow that capex spending, that will help to free cash flow at Amazon, Microsoft and Google. At the same time, if data center pauses prove fatal to neoclouds, the hyperscalers will have less competition in the market for AI compute. That could provide a boost to their margins. This could be true even for a company like Apple that isn’t in the cloud business. The iPhone maker has been forced to raise prices on its products largely due to the scarcity of memory chips, which are being gobbled up by the growth in AI data centers. If that data center growth slows, memory prices could stabilize or fall, which would be a welcome development at Apple. Its shares rose more than 6% on Wednesday. A black eye for Elon Musk, but how bad? No matter what you think of Musk’s accomplishments as a tech visionary and businessman, Tuesday’s results made it pretty clear his eye-popping investments in political races since Trump reentered the White House have backfired. He reportedly donated nearly $450 million to back Republican candidates in the midterm elections, a significant chunk of it in Texas, where his most important companies, SpaceX and Tesla, are based. Last year, he and allied groups pumped around $20 million into a Wisconsin Supreme Court race, an effort that flopped when the Trump-endorsed candidate, Brad Schimel, lost. But other than hurting his reputation as a player in electoral politics, it isn’t clear just how bad the blue wave will be for Musk’s businesses. Shares of SpaceX and Tesla dropped more than 4% and 2%, respectively, on Wednesday. Data center moratoriums could trip up future projects at SpaceX, which has quietly become a meaningful provider of AI compute to Anthropic and other customers. But you could also argue that no tech company stands to benefit more from an (improbable) total ban on data centers than SpaceX because of its efforts to put AI compute in space. Not only is SpaceX building its own constellation of orbital data centers, it also dominates the commercial rocket launching business that will allow other companies like Google to lob their own AI compute into space. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote on X late Tuesday night. SpaceX’s dominance of rocket launches also makes it unlikely that Democrats can do real damage to SpaceX’s government contracts without seriously undercutting U.S. ambitions in space. Democratic members of Congress certainly could make Musk’s life unpleasant by constantly calling him to testify or by probing his dealings with the government or his oversight of the Department of Government Efficiency. In Texas, the Democratic governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, made Musk’s tax breaks from and contracts with the state and his relationship with her Republican opponent, Greg Abbott, a centerpiece of her campaign. Still, how likely is it that Hinojosa goes on the offensive to stop SpaceX-Tesla projects in the state, such as their Terafab semiconductor manufacturing facility? Doing anything that kills Texas jobs could blow up in her face and interrupt her political ascendancy. A crypto bloodbath. An unsung storyline Tuesday night was how resoundingly the election drove nails into the coffin of crypto’s legislative aspirations. The blockchain industry spent more than $40 million in 2024 to unseat Sherrod Brown, the Democratic senator from Ohio who oversaw the Senate Banking Committee. But Brown clawed his way back to office on Tuesday night in a special election, despite the crypto industry’s top super PAC spending $46 million on ads. Some onlookers have speculated that Brown could end up with oversight of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the small regulatory agency charged with supervising prediction markets and many crypto assets. With Elizabeth Warren likely to assume the chair of the Senate Banking Committee, two of the industry’s leading critics could have leadership roles in the next Congress. As a result, not only will the crypto industry’s hope for its flagship Clarity Act evaporate, but the industry will likely face a reckoning for its close ties to the Trump administration amid an onslaught of oversight hearings and investigations. Back on the campaign trail. While the 2028 presidential election is still two years away, the cycle starts now, according to Kovacevich. That means prospective candidates are beginning to sharpen their talking points around AI, and groups like Kovacevich’s are vying to help shape their platforms. In 2025, Chamber of Progress launched the Blue Horizon Project, an initiative to “restore tech optimism” to the Democratic Party. It is headed by Dave Vorland, a former senior official in the Biden administration’s Department of Defense. Kovacevich said the Blue Horizon Project has already met with the staff of would-be candidates, though he declined to name any, and is hiring a consultant to help engage directly with candidates. “I’ve been encouraged that a lot of the 2028 field is taking a pretty measured approach,” he said. “There aren’t that many who have called for a ban on superintelligence or data centers.” Carney is heading a similar group, Project Blueprint, created by Democratic megadonor and venture capitalist Ron Conway and announced in September. Carney said he’s met with a number of people who are likely to run for president and wants to help them work through their campaign platforms. He said the requirement shouldn’t be to have a 100-point plan on AI, especially given how fast the technology is moving, but that candidates should know what they’re talking about and have a positive message. Carney said the only times a negative, divisive message has won the presidency were in 2016 and 2024. “Not to get sentimental about my old boss, but I think that’s what people are really craving, and that includes AI. It can’t just be the industry is bad and tech is bad, and it can’t just be, ‘Get out of my way, we know better.’”

title: How Smaller Banks Are Giving Agents Access to Accounts
content: Greetings! When it comes to letting your AI agent—such as Muse or Instinct—manage your personal finances or go shopping, your choice of bank will make a big difference. Some of the biggest banks in the U.S., like JPMorgan, are restricting AI agents’ access to consumers’ personal bank accounts, saying letting them in is too risky. But some smaller banks are going in the opposite direction, giving AI assistants more access to consumer banking which they see as a potential area of growth. That includes Lead Bank, a Kansas City, Missouri-based bank that works with fintechs like Stripe, a major payment provider for AI agent apps. Increase Bank, owned by fintech entrepreneur and early Stripe employee Darragh Buckley, is planning to offer banking for agents too, along with cards that agents can use. These banks are conscious of the risks. Lead Bank allows its fintech partners to issue bank account numbers for customers, reserved for AI agents. That in turn enables the agents to perform banking tasks like moving money through ACH and wire transfers while allowing the customers to limit what the agents can do in their accounts. The bank also says it has controls including transaction and spending limits and can immediately lock an agent out from the account if needed. “This ensures agents can only move money within explicitly defined parameters, rather than having unrestricted access to customer funds,” a spokesperson for Lead Bank said. In the case of Increase Bank, it plans to offer isolated bank accounts for agents that will be separate from the rest of the human customer's money, and the customer will be able to decide which agents can access the account. The agent would be able to access its account through an API, with Increase Bank confirming that the agent has permission. “We don’t need the entire industry to coordinate banking for agents. It's sufficient to have just a small cohort of technology-forward banks” to enable agents to get bank accounts, said Buckley, who already set up a personal bank account at Increase Bank in his name for his agent. Then there’s Natural, a payment startup backed by venture firm Forerunner that has raised over $40 million in total. Natural is bringing banking products such as payments and credit lines to AI agents. Natural isn’t a bank but it’s offering a way for digital wallets used by agents to hold money in an FDIC-insured account. Natural uses Column Bank to hold the money, and each wallet is a sub-ledger into customers’ individual accounts. Natural in turn offers its digital wallet to AI companies to use in agents, enabling the agents to send and request money. For example, Natural works with Conduit, a startup that offers AI agents used by short-term rentals and hotels to help manage their businesses. With the digital wallets, Conduit’s agents can accept payments, pay vendors and contractors, and store money. Banks are also helping agents make payments by issuing one-time use virtual cards, which helps keep the agents from accidentally splurging. Cross River Bank, which works closely with payments giant Stripe, said agent card payments powered by the bank have reached more than $40 million across over 200,000 transactions over the past three months, with airlines being the top consumer spend category. Still, letting AI agents into consumer banking raises questions about liability and cybersecurity—if an agent makes a payment a customer didn’t intend, for example, it’s unclear who is on the hook for reimbursing the customer. Wells Fargo, for its part, has warned it could restrict or block some AI tools and recently updated its terms to say that if a customer uses an AI agent to access their bank accounts, the customer is responsible for the agents’ actions. But Natural co-founder and CEO Kahlil Lalji argues that banks trying to block agents face an uphill battle. Agents with access to a user’s personal email can still see things like verification codes to log in, making them hard to keep out. In his view, banks and fintechs are better off giving agents access in a way that makes the agents’ activities easy to track and manage. “The only path out is through, then give agents a scoped access to do everything that they’re going to want to do, where at least you can audit and verify that you understand what’s going on,” Lalji said. “Big banks can’t do that technologically, so their protection is close up or try and close up.” New From Our Reporters Apollo Is Vastly Outspending the Neoclouds on AI Chips By Dakin Campbell Politics and Policy Blue Wave Could Engulf Data Center Industry By  Shane Burke Exclusive Anthropic Touts Claude’s Chip Design Skills to IPO Investors By Qianer Liu, Valida Pau and Phoebe Liu

content: The Pentagon, in another illustration of its hopes to erode China’s dominance of the drone revolution, is making a $450 million conditional loan to U.S. drone juggernaut Neros Technologies and has also taken an equity stake in the startup. Soren Monroe-Anderson, the 23-year-old CEO of Torrance, Calif.–based Neros, told me he will use the money to build out a vertically integrated factory making virtually all the company’s own drone components, including battery packs. The loan, announced Monday, is the second such award by the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, its investment arm. In July, the OSC made an $820 million conditional loan to Performance Drone Works, an Alabama maker of drone components. The loans are part of a massive push by the Pentagon to build up the U.S.’s drone-making capabilities and its inventory of the aircraft. Last month, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the Pentagon was asking Congress for a total of $100 billion over the next year for its drone ambitions. Even with such a gargantuan cash effort, the Pentagon will have difficulty matching China’s formidable dominance in the production of drones and the components that go into them. One Chinese company—DJI—sells about three-quarters of the world’s drones, including those used by both sides in the Ukraine war. The Pentagon’s proposed fiscal 2027 budget includes $53 billion for its Drone Dominance program, which involves a series of competitions that require participants not only to produce high-performing drones, but to develop the capacity to manufacture them at high volume and fast. Neros, which Monroe-Anderson co-founded just three years ago, has dominated the competitions. In both the first and second phases of the program, the Pentagon pulled drone orders awarded to other companies and gave them to Neros because it had demonstrated the capacity to quickly manufacture the aircraft in the thousands. In the second phase, Neros was the only participant to place in both of the competition categories. Neros finished first in the Close Quarters Battle category—in which the drones had to complete a mission in confined spaces, like buildings, where GPS did not necessarily work—and third in the Deep Strike category. Now Monroe-Anderson said Neros is gearing up for the competition’s third phase , which toughens the missions participants must complete. Winners will share $450 million in orders for about 60,000 drones, with the possibility of bonus orders totaling 40,000 additional drones. A Pentagon spokesperson told me that all nine companies that placed in the second phase will advance to the new phase. Monroe-Anderson said Neros so far is the only participant that will compete in both competition categories. Neros has been on a tear. In 2023, Monroe-Anderson, a former champion drone racer, got obsessed with helping Ukraine fight its war against Russia, which invaded the country the previous year. He and co-founder Olaf Hichwa, another former drone racer, started tinkering with drones in the home of Hichwa’s parents. They began attempting to sell those drones to Ukraine, initially getting rebuffed but eventually supplying them to the country in the thousands. In 2025 and this year, Neros has landed a series of big military contracts, including a $17 million order from the Marine Corps and a $500 million order from the Army. In August, the startup raised $250 million in a Series C round at a $2.5 billion valuation. Monroe-Anderson said the OSC, the Pentagon investment arm, contacted him around February to open discussions about the loan and an equity investment. He said he and Hichwa last year decided to raise the company’s current production of roughly 100,000 drones per year to 1 million by 2028. They also want to vertically integrate, not just assemble components bought from suppliers. As we have previously reported , one of Neros’ main suppliers is Unusual Machines and its Upgrade Energy battery division. Monroe-Anderson said Neros wants to manufacture its own electric motors, along with other electronic components, battery packs and frames. Later, Neros wants to make its own chips. The OSC officials listened to Neros’ plans and said, “Yeah, that’s pretty much exactly what we’ve been thinking needs to happen for the country for drone production,” Monroe-Anderson said. “When OSC reached out to us, I think it was a very clear matchup from the get-go because we just basically added details of what our vision already was,” he said. The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Neros was speaking with the Pentagon about an equity investment.

title: Cerebras’ Lockups Hold a Lesson for Anthropic Employees
content: Even before Wednesday’s election-driven sell-off in tech stocks, Cerebras shares had fallen sharply since its initial public offering six months ago. That’s bad news for investors who bought at the IPO as well as employees who hung on to their newly public shares. But those insiders needn’t have gotten burned. Cerebras offered them the chance to sell much of their stock at various times over the past six months, which is unlike how newly public companies typically operate. The outcome holds a lesson for the employees of Anthropic, which like Cerebras has instituted a staggered schedule for when insiders can sell shares. The lesson: Take some money off the table as soon as you can. To recap: Cerebras, a designer of specialized AI chips, went public in May at a valuation of $56 billion . After it priced the offering at $185, shares soared to more than $311 at the end of the first day of trading, earning a round of congratulations for the company’s founders as well as investors such as Benchmark Capital, Foundational Capital and Eclipse Capital. But shares have sunk since then to around $92, dragged down by a quarterly update that disclosed the company’s hardware sales had fallen. Cerebras’ rank-and-file employees are likely disappointed—especially since they’ve given up some of their shares to cover the taxes owed to the government when the shares vested. Here’s how it worked: Restricted stock units granted to employees when Cerebras was a private company became common stock—4.8 million shares in total—on the day of the IPO, according to its prospectus. The vesting of those stock units counted as taxable income for employees, and were taxed at the IPO price of $185. To cover the taxes, Cerebras kept about 2.25 million of those shares and paid more than $416 million to the IRS on employees’ behalf, according to its securities filings. That’s known as net share settlement, a common practice for companies going public. “The reason companies do that is they’re able to peg the tax liability to the IPO price,” said Ran Ben-Tzur, co-chair of the capital markets group at Fenwick & West. That makes it easier for the company and the employee to figure out how much they owe in taxes. Having to fork over taxes at a $185 per share value must be galling for employees, given that the stock is currently trading at around half that level. But while many companies prevent their employees from selling shares in the first six months, Cerebras didn’t. Rank-and-file employees at Cerebras have been allowed to sell their stock in 11 windows, starting with the first day of trading and extending through the end of October. By then, the stock had dropped to under $110. When Cerebras reports its third-quarter earnings on November 9, it will unlock another 21.5% of stock held by nonexecutive employees. If they sold shares in the past few months above the $185 IPO price, employees would have to pay capital gains taxes. If they sold below $185, they take a capital loss that can offset taxes on other gains—up to $3,000 of ordinary income. All told, the staggered lockup should have helped Cerebras employees—as long as they’ve started to sell. That’s an important takeaway as we head into the public listing of Anthropic, which has an even more complicated lockup structure than Cerebras. Significantly, Anthropic’s plan includes the ability for insiders to start selling up to 10% of their shares on their first trading days. That will be a tempting opportunity for some, particularly since they’ll start paying taxes on their stock at the IPO. As with Cerebras, Anthropic has said it plans to use the IPO to cover the tax obligations on employees’ RSUs. title: Lumentum Sell-Off After Marvell Offer Raises Chance of Alternate Bid
content: Lumentum, the optical networking component maker that Marvell Technology said on Monday it would buy, was swept up by Wednesday’s election-driven sell-off of stocks that have benefited most from the AI data center boom. But investors shouldn’t lose sight of the bigger picture—another bidder for Lumentum could emerge, or Marvell could come back and sweeten its proposal with more cash. Marvell’s proposed all-stock acquisition of Lumentum—which as of Tuesday valued the firm at around $80 billion—shone a spotlight on the latter’s position in a promising corner of the AI infrastructure market. Optical technology, such as the lasers Lumentum makes, moves data within and between data centers faster than the copper wiring traditionally used in these facilities. The pressures of AI computing make faster data transmission vital. Wall Street didn’t receive Marvell’s deal well, likely because the chip designer was proposing to increase the number of its outstanding shares by roughly 50% to buy Lumentum. Even before Wednesday’s sell-off, Marvell’s stock had fallen 32% since news of the deal leaked a week ago. That had reduced the value put on Lumentum from $115 billion to $78 billion. Wednesday’s sell-off shrank the value to about $71 billion. (Marvell was talking about Lumentum’s enterprise value but because Lumentum has only about $500 million of net cash, the difference between its market capitalization and enterprise value is negligible.) Lumentum shares fell 10% on Wednesday, continuing a steady decline over the past few weeks, as worries about a data center slowdown have mounted. At its current price of $610, Lumentum is trading about $100 a share below the value of Marvell’s offer, suggesting investors don’t believe the bid will close. But Lumentum will remain hugely valuable whatever happens. Even if AI-related demand drops off—as a result of new state bans on data center development or slowing investment—Lumentum and other optical interconnect firms should still grow, although perhaps not as fast. Even for non-AI computing or simple web hosting, companies are demanding higher performance and greater bandwidth, a trend that should ensure Lumentum’s continued relevance as a key component supplier as optical networking expands. “As we go to generations of Nvidia [graphics processing units] that are going to [come out] faster and faster over the next 10 years, the move from copper to optics to photonics” is going to be a big tailwind for companies that make optical equipment across the board, said David Vogt, an equity analyst at UBS who covers semiconductor networking stocks. It’s possible another company will emerge with a rival bid for Lumentum. Potential bidders include AMD, Intel and maybe even Nvidia. All three make chips for data centers and for networking technology that moves data between servers. All three could benefit from acquiring optical technology. “You’ve got to remember these companies are now providing rack-scale solutions, not just component solutions,” said Jim McGregor, co-founder and analyst at tech research firm Tirias Research, referring to the chipmakers’ shift from simply selling individual chips to selling entire server racks, equipped with networking gear to string those chips together. While those companies could bid for other optical equipment providers, such as Coherent or Applied Optoelectronics, Lumentum is unique in the type of laser it sells, according to McGregor, so much so that it sells its advanced lasers to other firms in the optical sector. Coherent, for instance, buys some lasers from Lumentum in addition to making some of its own. Coherent makes the finished devices that enable fiber-optic cables to transmit data by converting electrical signals into light. Wall Street analysts expect Lumentum’s revenue growth to accelerate to 122% in the year to June as it sells more of its optical components to firms looking for ways to pipe large volumes of data between servers that are faster than the copper wiring currently most prevalent. In contrast, analysts are projecting 50% growth at Coherent in the year to June and over 100% growth at Applied Optoelectronics over the next couple of years. But Lumentum has a gross margin of nearly 50%, far above the others. That gives it a premium valuation. As of Tuesday’s close, it was trading at 8 times analyst estimates of the companies’ forward revenue, well above the multiples of 3 to 4 at which Applied Optoelectronics and Coherent are trading, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Lumentum’s premium position, and Wall Street’s tepid reaction to Marvell’s offer, might persuade rivals to try to beat Marvell’s all-stock bid. If a rival bidder can offer cash in addition to stock, it likely would draw interest from Lumentum shareholders. That could force Marvell to revise its own offer to include cash. Nvidia, to be sure, might be less inclined to bid against Marvell because it already has a stake in both Marvell and Lumentum, having invested $2 billion in each company earlier this year when it signed purchase agreements to buy their products. Marvell, which counts some of AI’s biggest spenders such as Amazon and Microsoft as customers, won’t likely give up Lumentum without a fight. Marvell has been locked in a yearslong race with its larger rival, Broadcom, to win business from large tech companies looking to reduce their dependence on pricey AI chips from their shared rival, Nvidia. Buying Lumentum could help with that, according to Tirias’ McGregor. “Broadcom has an end-to-end solution that goes all the way from the networking equipment…down to the copackaged optics. They’ve got pretty much everything in-house. If they don’t, they’ve got partners for it, and they’re much bigger,” said McGregor. “Let’s face it: The two companies compete in networking. The two companies compete in custom silicon. The two companies compete in several areas, but Broadcom is the 800-pound gorilla, so it makes sense why Marvell is trying to at least expand in” optical networking. McGregor drew a parallel between Marvell’s interest in Lumentum and networking firm Cisco, which during the 2000s internet boom fueled most of its growth through acquisitions. “It goes through waves. We just haven’t seen a lot of [acquisition interest] associated with optical, but that very much could change,” he said. The question is whether Marvell has the resources to fight a cash and stock offer from a rival. Its all-stock bid may not end up being good enough for Lumentum shareholders.

title: Blue Wave Could Engulf Data Center Industry
content: Election Day’s blue wave is set to crash into the data center industry. In 12 states, the winning or leading candidate for governor has called for a pause on data center development, including Alaska, Georgia, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Oregon, Texas and Wisconsin. And in even more states, winners have also pledged other restrictions on data centers including ratepayer protections, environmental limits and the elimination of tax incentives for building the facilities. And of the 24 incoming governors who did not call for a pause, 22 back at least one limit on data centers. Ratepayer protections, which would make sure households don’t shoulder the costs of increased power demand or energy infrastructure buildouts, were nearly universal: 34 of 36 winners support them. And 27 back restrictions relating to water usage or the environment. Fifteen leading candidates say they would cut or end the tax breaks that states have used to court developers. (For a detailed pre-election analysis of the data center positions of state candidates, see this story .) Governor candidates calling for data center pauses lost races in nine states, but only a few of these races were ever close. Florida was the tightest toss-up, and a key battleground on the issue. Republican Byron Donalds, who opposed a statewide pause and was backed by millions in spending from super PACs affiliated with Anthropic and OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, beat Democrat David Jolly by about a percentage point. Some of the states where winning candidates would restrict data centers are at the center of the industry’s building plans. OpenAI’s Stargate project with Oracle has massive sites in Texas, Michigan and New Mexico. SoftBank’s SB Energy plans to build an 8-gigawatt campus for OpenAI in Ohio. Microsoft, Amazon and Nvidia have lined up Texas sites . In Georgia, the Atlanta metro area has overtaken Northern Virginia as the busiest market for data center construction, according to real estate firm CBRE. In an interview on The Information’s TITV on Wednesday, Charles Hua, founder and executive director of Power Lines, a nonprofit focused on energy regulation, said that the election results in Ohio, Texas and Georgia were particularly noteworthy. “Those are three of the fastest growing markets for data center development for electricity demand growth and and all three saw pretty dramatic outcomes that folks maybe weren’t actually expecting,” Hua said. How (and whether) governors put in place their moratoriums will vary—in duration, strictness and path of action. But the narrowing map could lead to higher costs and more red tape for the data center and AI industries. It introduces even more uncertainty for investors about the payoff on the large AI investments of big tech firms. If neoclouds and other data center developers can’t turn borrowed money into revenue quickly enough, the delay could ripple, with developers paying interest on buildings that are not earning rent, lenders waiting longer to be repaid and AI companies going without the computing power they’ve committed to buy. Some deals could unravel entirely, if missed deadlines give tenants the rights to terminate. SB Energy warned in its IPO filing that permit delays could lead to this at OpenAI’s Ohio campus. Even if data centers weren’t the deciding issue in elections, the sweep matches American public opinion. In an August poll from Pew Research Center, six in 10 U.S. adults said they would be uncomfortable with a new one operating in their area, with more than half calling them bad for the environment and half considering them bad for home energy costs. Few saw a bright side: Less than a quarter agreed they would be good for local jobs or tax revenue. The moratoriums would join more than 500 data center pauses or bans at the local level, as shown by The Information’s ban tracker . At the year’s start, only about 40 towns and counties had bans in place. By August, the count had topped 500, driven by worries about power bills, water usage, noise and blight.

The Download: Texas’s fragile AI boom and energy policy shifts
Plus: America’s data center boom has hit a political wall.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.
Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat, Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor, and Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. They won after making data centers a central issue on the campaign trail.
The swings could spell trouble for hyperscalers with ambitious plans in the state. They also add to growing anxiety that America’s AI buildout could stall.
Here’s how the election results could reshape AI’s future.
—James O'Donnell
What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
Democrats have taken control of both the House and the Senate, but we probably won’t see major federal climate and energy legislation while Trump remains president. The midterm elections could, however, be a big deal for energy at the state and local level.
The results could shape everything from the state grid and data center development to renewable energy and greenhouse gas emissions.
Find out what the midterms could mean for the future of US energy.
—Casey Crownhart
This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.
On November 9, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). It’s a plan that could start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved. But some environmental groups oppose the bill, or parts of it.
Explore the trade-offs behind America's proposed permitting overhaul.

The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

2 Blood banks have become the latest victims of fridge hacks

+ Experts are split over who’s behind the attacks. (BBC)
3 Democrats are preparing to investigate Elon Musk
His firms have won over $16 billion in government contracts. (NPR)
+ His unprecedented spending may even have hurt Republicans. (Atlantic $)
+ Texas’s blue wave has rattled Musk and SpaceX. (Ars Technica)
4 The new Congress could challenge Trump’s science cuts
But he can still veto any bills they pass. (Nature)
+ Trump has already dealt many blows to science. (MIT Technology Review)
5 China is luring AI expertise in while blocking it from leaving
It just blocked SoftBank’s bid for ABB Robotics. (WSJ $)
+ Its chipmakers are poaching engineers from foreign rivals. (CNBC)
+ A star mathematician has left the US to develop AI in China. (SCMP)
6 Watchdogs have sued over tech titans advising the Pentagon
Musk and Palmer Luckey could profit from their advice. (Military.com)
7 New research tests whether AI knows its own “thoughts”
It’s trying to map out AI’s capacity for introspection. (Quanta)

—Greg Casar, a Democratic congressman from Texas, tells Wired that the backlash against data centers could herald a much bigger political fight over AI.
One more thing
Meet the radio-obsessed civilian shaping Ukraine’s drone defense
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov is, at least unofficially, a spy. Once a month, he drives to the frontline in a VW van equipped with radio hardware, roof antennas, and devices that monitor drones. Over several days, he searches the skies for transmissions that can help Ukrainian troops.
Drones define this brutal conflict, and most rely on the radio communications Flash has obsessed over since childhood. Though now a civilian, the former officer has taken it upon himself to inform his country’s defense on all matters related to radio.
Unlike traditional spies, Flash shares his discoveries with over 127,000 followers—including soldiers and officials—on social media. His work has won fans in the military, but also sparked controversy among the top brass. Read the full story.

A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
The midterms are over, and the next big fight could be over permitting reform.
A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.
With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9. It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform. People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years.
The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.
The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines. Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated.
So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up. The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense.)
One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables. So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it.
The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats. The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP.
Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.
Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it. An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands.
Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels. The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically.
A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US. One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040. In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same.
Another report, from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury.
But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants. As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced.
“You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.
To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline. Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased.
This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control. It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board. Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers. But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.
In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too. And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall.
Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal. But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.

title: Fraunhofer ITWM auf der Supercomputing 2026: High Performance Computing wird smarter und energieeffizienter
content:
Fraunhofer ITWM auf der Supercomputing 2026: High Performance Computing wird smarter und energieeffizienter
Hinweis zur Verwendung von Bildmaterial: Die Verwendung des Bildmaterials zur Pressemitteilung ist bei Nennung der Quelle vergütungsfrei gestattet.
